title: Application for Partition of Land
explainer:

Munir had successfully applied for partition of jointly-owned land, and a Tehsildar approved it, leading to a mutation (revenue record change) in his favor. The other co-owner objected, claiming the order was obtained improperly and that the official lacked jurisdiction to decide the matter. She challenged the partition through a civil suit and also filed an appeal before the Additional Commissioner (Revenue), which was still pending. Since the matter was still sub judice before the appropriate revenue and civil forums, it ruled that pursuing a criminal corruption inquiry at this stage was unjustified and appeared aimed at pressuring Munir into a compromise. title: Jurisdiction of Federal Ombudsman is limited
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over a petrol pump property in Islamabad that had been leased by the Capital Development Authority (CDA) to a Staff Welfare Committee, which in turn sub-leased it to a tenant. Over several years, the tenant fought eviction through multiple courts, all the way up to the Supreme Court of Pakistan, which ultimately ruled against him. Despite this final resolution, a complaint was filed with the Federal Ombudsman (Wafaqi Mohtasib), who issued an order halting the auction of the property, effectively reopening a matter the courts had already settled.

The petitioner challenged this before the Islamabad High Court, arguing that the Ombudsman had no authority to intervene once the courts, including the Supreme Court, had finally decided the matter. The court agreed, ruling that the Ombudsman's jurisdiction is limited and does not extend to reviewing or overturning issues already conclusively resolved by courts of law. The court quashed the Ombudsman's proceedings and orders as illegal and without jurisdiction, and directed the CDA Chairman to supervise a fresh, transparent auction of the property in line with procurement rules.

This judgment matters because it clarifies the boundaries of the Ombudsman's power, confirming that this office cannot act as an appellate authority over matters already finally decided by the judiciary. It reinforces the principle that court judgments, especially those of the Supreme Court, must be respected and cannot be revisited by administrative bodies like the Ombudsman.

title: Jurisdiction of Family Courts and FOSPAH
explainer:
This case concerns a property dispute between a husband and wife arising from their marriage contract (nikahnama), and which forum has the legal authority to decide it. After their marriage broke down, the wife filed a complaint claiming her dower rights, including a promised 10-marla house or its equivalent, under women's property rights laws. Her complaint was eventually taken up by the Federal Ombudsman Secretariat for Protection Against Harassment of Women at Workplace in Islamabad, which allowed her to file an amended, more detailed complaint about the property. The husband challenged this, arguing the Ombudsman lacked jurisdiction, especially since related suits between the same parties (including one on divorce and one on cancelling nikahnama clauses) were already pending in Family and Civil Courts in Peshawar.

The Islamabad High Court ruled in favor of the husband. It held that no specific property had actually been identified or was traceable within Islamabad, so the Ombudsman could not compel handover of any property. More importantly, the Court found that the Family Courts Act, 1964 is the comprehensive law governing such matters, giving Family Courts exclusive jurisdiction over ten specified categories of disputes, including a wife's personal property claims. This law overrides other forums, including the women's property rights ombudsman mechanism, when the matter falls within its scope. The petition was allowed, meaning the Ombudsman's order was set aside.

This case matters because it clarifies that disputes over a wife's property claims arising from marriage should generally go to Family Cour

title: Review Jurisdiction of Supreme Court
explainer:
This case is about the well-known Mukhtar Mai matter, which involved a gang-rape ordered by a tribal jirga in Punjab. After the original criminal case went through the trial court, the Lahore High Court, and finally the Supreme Court (which in 2011 upheld the acquittal of most accused, keeping only one man convicted with life imprisonment), Mukhtar Mai asked the Supreme Court to review its own 2011 judgment.

Her lawyer raised several questions, such as how much corroboration a rape victim's testimony needs, whether a virgin and a divorced woman should be treated differently as witnesses, how confessions made during cross-examination should be treated, the guilt of jirga members who allow such crimes, and whether DNA evidence should be strictly required in remote rural cases.

The Supreme Court explained that a review petition is not the same as an appeal. It cannot be used to reopen and reassess the evidence or reach a different conclusion than the original judgment. Review is only allowed in rare situations involving an obvious, glaring mistake of law or fact on the face of the record—not simply because someone believes the earlier decision was wrong.

Since all the arguments raised required re-examining the evidence rather than pointing to any clear, self-evident error, the Court held they could not be considered under its limited review jurisdiction. The review petitions were therefore dismissed, leaving the 2011 judgment intact.

title: Re-Examination Allowed by Islamabad High Court
explainer:
This case comes from the Islamabad High Court and involves a criminal revision petition arising out of an abduction case registered under Section 365-A of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with kidnapping for ransom. The complainant, whose father had been abducted, had given evidence in court but had not been asked about certain details concerning how ransom money was paid, even though this information had already come up during the police investigation. The complainant asked the trial court to let him be recalled so he could add this missing information to his statement. The Anti-Terrorism Court allowed this request under Section 540 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which lets a court recall or re-examine a witness if doing so is essential to reaching a fair decision.

The accused challenged this decision, arguing that letting the witness be recalled would unfairly improve the prosecution's case and fill gaps that should benefit the defence instead.

The High Court disagreed and dismissed the petition. It held that the missing information about the ransom payment was not being used to patch a weak spot in the prosecution's case, but was necessary for arriving at a just and complete decision. The court emphasized that recalling witnesses to serve justice is not just allowed but sometimes required by law, and that cases should be decided on their merits rather than technical objections. This ruling reinforces courts' broad power to ensure all relevant facts are properly presented before reaching a verdict.

title: If any relief was omitted then civil servant was debarred from claiming
explainer:
This case involved employees of the National Highway Authority who filed appeals with the Federal Service Tribunal seeking multiple types of relief in a single case, including increases in personal pay, upgrading their job positions, changes to promotion quotas, amendments to service rules, more available job seats, and reduction of income disparity between different service classes.

The National Highway Authority objected, arguing that employees could not claim more than one relief in a single appeal and that the Tribunal had no power to order changes to service rules.

The Tribunal rejected both objections. It ruled that when multiple claims arise from the same underlying grievance (cause of action), all of them should be raised together in one case, similar to the rule in civil courts under the Code of Civil Procedure. If a person leaves out a valid claim, they lose the right to raise it separately later. Since all the employees relief requests stemmed from the same core dispute, combining them in one appeal was proper, not improper.

The Tribunal also held that it did have authority, under Article 212 of the Constitution, to strike down or direct amendment of service rules if those rules violated an employee's basic rights, and to address disparities in pay and treatment among government employees, since the Constitution requires fair conditions and reduced income disparity.

This ruling clarifies that civil servants may combine all related claims in one appeal, and that service tribunals have real power to challenge unfair service rules, not just individual employment decisions.

title: Cancellation of Mutation without Jurisdiction
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between the National Highways Authority (NHA) and Punjab government revenue officials over land along the Grand Trunk Road and other highways. In 2002, the Punjab government transferred control of the "right of way" along these roads to NHA, unconditionally and free of cost, with mutations (land revenue records) to be updated in NHA's name. Later, in 2004-2005, Punjab officials reversed course, calling the earlier wording a typographical error, and directed District Officers to cancel the mutations and restore ownership to the provincial government. Land leased out by NHA to private parties, including a building plan, was also cancelled and occupants ordered removed. NHA and affected lessees challenged these cancellations, arguing they were carried out without proper authority and without giving them any notice or hearing.

The Lahore High Court found that whether the government had legal authority to cancel the mutations, and whether proper procedures were followed originally, were factual questions requiring evidence, not something the court could resolve on a writ petition. However, it ruled that canceling the mutations without notifying or hearing the affected parties violated basic principles of natural justice. The court set aside the cancellation orders and sent the matter back to the District Officers (Revenue) to decide afresh, this time after properly hearing all parties involved. This case matters because it reinforces that government cannot strip people of property rights through unilateral orders without giving them a chance to be heard.

title: Special Statute over Arbitration - Jurisdiction of Rent Controller
explainer:
This case is about whether a landlord-tenant dispute governed by a rent law can be diverted to arbitration because the lease agreement contained an arbitration clause.

The landlords had leased land in Islamabad to the tenants for ten years, extendable by mutual consent. After the lease period ended, the landlords filed an eviction petition before the Rent Controller under the Islamabad Rent Restriction Ordinance, 2001. The tenants responded by asking the Rent Controller to stay those proceedings under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, arguing that the dispute should instead be resolved through arbitration as stated in the lease agreement. The Rent Controller rejected this request, and a single judge of the Islamabad High Court upheld that decision. The tenants then appealed to a two-judge bench.

The High Court dismissed the appeal. It held that while parties are generally free to agree to arbitration for contractual disputes, when a special law like the Rent Ordinance specifically governs a particular matter such as tenant eviction, that special law must be followed exclusively. Arbitration cannot override the Rent Controller's jurisdiction in eviction matters. Even if a lease contains an arbitration clause, an eviction petition remains valid and must be decided by the Rent Controller, not an arbitrator.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that specialized statutory forums, like Rent Controllers, retain exclusive authority over matters within their specific domain, and general arbitration agreements cannot be used to bypass them.

title: PLJ 2015 Peshawar 392 (DB)
explainer:

The Family Court and District Judge in Charsadda had partly ruled against her, holding that her claim for the unpaid portion of her dower was filed too late, beyond the three-year limitation period set by Article 103 of the Limitation Act, 1908, which normally runs from when dower is demanded and refused.

During reconciliation proceedings, the husband sought dissolution through khula. The Family Court dissolved the marriage on that basis and then decided the remaining disputes, partly favoring the wife on dowry articles but denying her maintenance and dower claims. Both parties appealed, and the Appellate Court modified the decision, granting the wife maintenance for her iddat period (the waiting period after divorce) and dowry articles or their cash equivalent.

The husband challenged this decision in the High Court, arguing the maintenance award and dowry valuation were wrong, and that his wife should return the dower since the marriage ended by khula.

The Lahore High Court upheld the lower courts' findings, ruling that factual findings by competent courts cannot be disturbed under constitutional petitions unless there is serious injustice, which was not shown here. title: Leave to Appeal in a Guardian Case
explainer:
This case concerns a custody dispute over a young girl, Najla Bugti, following her parents' divorce. After the divorce, the mother (the appellant) kept custody of the child but later remarried a man unrelated to Najla and moved from Quetta to Rawalpindi. The father then applied to be made the child's legal guardian under the Guardians and Wards Act, arguing that under Islamic law the mother loses her right to custody (Hizanat) once she remarries someone who is a stranger to the child. The Family Court and Additional District Judge sided with the father, and the Balochistan High Court upheld that decision. The mother appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing the father had failed to pay maintenance for the child and that a mother's loss of custody rights upon remarriage is not an absolute rule.

The Supreme Court disagreed with the mother's appeal. It found that the father had, in fact, been providing maintenance, and this was not seriously disputed in evidence. The Court reaffirmed that while a father is generally the natural guardian, the child's welfare is always the deciding factor in custody cases. It also held that under Islamic law, a mother's right to custody ends when she remarries a man unrelated to the child within prohibited degrees, unless special circumstances show the child's welfare still lies with her. Since no such exceptional circumstances existed here, the Court dismissed the mother's appeal, confirming custody with the father. The case highlights how courts balance legal rules on guardianship with the central principle of the child's best interests.

title: Constitutional Petition in a Christian Divorce Case
explainer:
This case involved a Christian couple from Quetta. After their marriage in 2006, the wife alleged that her husband began mistreating her and eventually turned her out of the house with their infant son in December 2007, without providing any financial support. She filed a suit seeking monthly maintenance for herself and the child under the Divorce Act, 1869, the law governing matters like marriage, divorce, and maintenance for Christians in Pakistan.

The trial court ordered the husband to pay Rs. 5,000 monthly to the wife and Rs. 2,000 for the child. On appeal, the amounts were adjusted to Rs. 3,000 for the wife and Rs. 2,500 for the child. The husband then challenged both decisions before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the trial court lacked jurisdiction and that the maintenance amount exceeded limits set by law, and that the evidence had not been properly evaluated.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It found that the husband had never raised the jurisdiction objection at the trial stage, so he could not raise it later. It also held that under the Divorce Act, a case can be filed wherever the spouses lived together, which applied here. Finally, the court found the maintenance amounts fixed by the lower courts were properly calculated in line with the law's requirements.

This case is significant because it confirms how Pakistani courts apply the Divorce Act, 1869 to determine maintenance rights for Christian spouses and children, and reinforces that legal objections not raised early in a case cannot be introduced later on app

title: HUMAN RIGHTS CASE NO. 5818 OF 2006 - ALLOTMENT OF RESIDENTIAL PLOTS
explainer:
Islamabad High Court dealt with a Human Rights Case that started after the Supreme Court took suo moto (on its own initiative) notice of a newspaper report. The report said the Prime Minister had directed that residential plots in Islamabad's Sector D-12 be allotted to Federal Secretaries and other senior grade-22 government officers, and that the scheme might be extended to more officials, including chief secretaries and police chiefs from various provinces.

The court examined whether this directive, and the Capital Development Authority's related actions, were lawful. It noted that while the government can grant benefits like housing to its employees as a matter of policy, it is under no constitutional or legal obligation to do so, and no civil servant has an automatic right to demand such a plot beyond their normal service terms. The court explained that judicial interference under Article 184(3) of the Constitution is reserved for exceptional cases involving violation of legal rights, not routine policy or administrative decisions made properly by the government using its discretion.

Finding that the plot allotment scheme had been approved and implemented within the bounds of law, without evidence of abuse of power or violation of anyone's legal rights, the court held that this case did not meet the threshold for judicial intervention. As a result, it dropped the suo moto proceedings, allowing the government's allotment decision to stand.

title: Remarriage can never be sole fact for deciding custody
explainer:
This case is about the custody of a young girl, born in 2008, after her parents' marriage ended in divorce. The father applied for custody, arguing that the mother had lost her right to it because she remarried a man unrelated to the child. Both the trial court and the appellate court sided with the father, mainly because of the mother's remarriage, and also directed that custody go to the child's paternal grandmother rather than the father himself.

The mother challenged this before the Lahore High Court. The Court ruled in her favor, holding that a mother's remarriage can never by itself decide custody; the real and overriding test under the law is the welfare of the child. It noted that the father had never genuinely sought custody and appeared to have filed the case mainly to counter a maintenance claim against him. The Court also held that custody could not simply be handed to a paternal grandmother while the child's own mother was alive and available, and stressed that a mother's natural love and care cannot be substituted by anyone else, especially for a growing daughter.

Finding that the lower courts had ignored the true legal test and focused solely on the remarriage, the High Court set aside their decisions and restored custody to the mother. The judgment reinforces the principle that child custody decisions in Pakistan must center on the child's best interests, not rigid or automatic rules based on a parent's remarriage.

title: Amended Challan can be presented in Court
explainer:
This case concerns a pharmaceutical company that manufactured an injectable drug later found to be substandard when tested by a government laboratory. The drug had been seized from a seller, who told the Drug Court he had purchased it from a distributor, who in turn said he obtained it from the manufacturing company under its warranty. Based on this chain, the Drug Court ordered that an amended complaint be filed adding the manufacturing company as an accused in the ongoing prosecution.

The company challenged this order in the Lahore High Court, arguing that once a formal charge sheet (challan) had been filed against a specific accused, no new accused could be added merely on the basis of a statement made in court, and that the investigating officer had never actually questioned or investigated the company itself.

The High Court agreed that the investigating Drug Inspector had failed to properly investigate the manufacturer before filing the challan, and that courts are meant to judge cases based on proper investigation, not conduct investigations themselves. Rather than simply approving the addition of the company as an accused, the Court ordered the investigating officer to reinvestigate the matter, formally involve the company, give it a chance to respond to the allegations, and then submit an amended challan within two months if the evidence supported it.

This case matters because it clarifies that amended charge sheets can be submitted later, but only after proper investigation and after giving the newly implicated party a fair opportunity to explain itself.

title: No Action Detrimental to Interest of any Person can be taken
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over who should run the All Pakistan Textile Mills Association (APTMA) after its Chairman's one-year term expired without a new election taking place. The Association's Managing Committee had passed a resolution saying that, until a new Chairman was elected, the Committee itself would manage affairs, with one member acting as convener. The government's Director Trade Organization cancelled this resolution, ruling it violated the Association's own governing rules, and instead directed that the Vice-Chairman should take charge. Members of the Managing Committee challenged this cancellation in the Lahore High Court.

The Court ruled in favor of the petitioners. It held that the Director's order was invalid because the Managing Committee members were never given a chance to be heard before their decision was overturned - a basic requirement of natural justice that must be followed before any action harmful to someone's interests is taken. The Court also found that, under the Association's own rules, when a Chairman's term ends without a new election, control should pass to the Managing Committee, not the Vice-Chairman as the Director had wrongly ordered. The Court set aside the Director's order to that extent and directed the Managing Committee to hold Chairman elections within two weeks.

This case matters because it reinforces that government officials cannot cancel decisions or take actions harming people's rights without first giving them a fair hearing, and it clarifies how internal succession disputes in trade organizations should be resolved according to their own constitutional documents.

title: Bail Granted on the ground of four days delay in lodging FIR
explainer:
This case involved a man named Altaf Hussain, alias Atti, who was accused of attempting to rape a young woman, the daughter of the person who filed the police complaint. He was charged under Pakistan's Penal Code sections dealing with rape and attempt to commit an offense, and was arrested. He then applied to the Lahore High Court's Multan Bench for post-arrest bail, asking to be released while the case proceeded.

The court granted him bail. It gave several reasons for this decision. First, the alleged victim was never taken for a medical examination, so there was no medical evidence confirming an attempted rape had occurred. Second, although the police report claimed the victim's clothes were torn and the string of her shalwar (a type of trouser) was broken, these torn clothes were never actually produced or shown to the investigating officer. Third, there was an unexplained four-day delay between the alleged incident and the filing of the police complaint, which the complainant did not account for.

Taken together, the court found these gaps cast serious doubt on the case against the petitioner at this stage. As a result, he was granted bail on furnishing bond of Rs. 50,000 with one surety. This case illustrates how delays in reporting crimes and lack of supporting evidence can influence bail decisions in serious criminal cases in Pakistan.

title: Physical presence of accused is not mandatory for 540-A Petition
explainer:
This case is about whether a person accused in a criminal trial must be physically present in court just to ask for an exemption from personal appearance under Section 540-A of the Criminal Procedure Code. The petitioner, working abroad, sought exemption from attending every court hearing in a fraud case pending against him, arguing it was inconvenient and expensive to travel. Two lower courts, the Ilaqa Qazi and the Additional Sessions Judge in Swat, refused his request, apparently believing he needed to appear in person first before being excused.

The Peshawar High Court disagreed and allowed his petition. It held that the wording of Section 540-A does not require an accused to be physically present before the court as a precondition for seeking exemption. The judge explained that laws should be interpreted based on their actual wording, not by adding requirements that were never written into them, and that criminal laws affecting personal liberty should be interpreted in favor of the accused when there is ambiguity. The court emphasized that the purpose of allowing exemptions is to let trials proceed smoothly without unnecessary obstruction, and that such exemptions should be granted liberally in genuine cases, while guarding against misuse.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that accused persons, especially those living or working abroad, are not forced into an unnecessary catch-22 of having to appear in person just to request excusal from future appearances, easing the practical burden on defendants while trials continue.

title: Succession of Tenant
explainer:
This case concerns a shop rented in Islamabad and a dispute over eviction proceedings under the Islamabad Rent Restriction Ordinance, 2001. The landlord filed an ejectment petition against the tenant for defaulting on rent payments. The tenant argued two main points: first, that when the eviction case was filed in January 2003, the Rent Controller lacked jurisdiction because the relevant notification bringing the property under the Ordinance only took effect later, in June 2004; and second, that he was not actually occupying the shop, so he should not be liable for rent.

The Supreme Court rejected both arguments. On jurisdiction, it held that since the Rent Controller acquired jurisdiction while the case was still pending, and no prejudice was caused to the tenant by deciding the case after that jurisdiction was acquired, the proceedings remained valid. On the occupancy issue, the Court explained that when a tenant dies, only the family members who continue actually living in or using the premises become the new statutory tenants, not just any legal heir. Since the petitioner himself was found to be in possession of the shop, he was rightly treated as the tenant liable for eviction.

The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, upholding the eviction order made by the Rent Controller and confirmed by the appellate court and the High Court. This case clarifies rules about jurisdiction timing and who qualifies as a tenant after the original tenant's death.

title: Quashment without moving 249-A and 265-K Petition
explainer:
This case involved two men, Agha Nadim and another petitioner, who ran a medicine trading business. A drug inspector had seized a batch of medicine from a shop in Vehari that was found by a government laboratory to be spurious, meaning it was not actually made by the company whose name appeared on it. Tracing the supply chain back through several sellers, the case eventually led to the petitioners' firm, and a criminal case was registered against them under drug laws.

The petitioners challenged this in the Lahore High Court, arguing that proper procedure had not been followed. They pointed out that the government board which permitted the case to be filed never issued them a show-cause notice or gave them a chance to respond, as required by the Punjab Drugs Rules. They also argued that two drug inspectors had been appointed to overlapping jurisdictions covering the same district, which was improper, and that they were never given the laboratory test report so they could challenge it as the law allowed.

The government argued the petitioners should first seek relief from the trial court under the ordinary criminal procedure code before approaching the High Court.

The court disagreed, ruling that petitioners need not first go to the trial court if the High Court is satisfied that continuing the case would amount to abuse of process. Finding that the required show-cause notice was never issued, the report was never supplied, and the inspector appointments were overlapping and unlawful, the court declared the case against the petitioners to be without lawful authority and quashed it.

The court used its constitutional and inherent powers to cancel (quash) the FIR and all related proceedings, rather than making him go through a lengthy trial court procedure. title: Quashment during Session Trial Judgment
explainer:
This case involved a criminal complaint that had led to an FIR being registered under Sections 324/34 of the Pakistan Penal Code (attempted murder). After investigation, the case (challan) was sent to the Sessions Court for trial. However, the Sessions Judge in Tank found the registration of the FIR to be doubtful and sent the case file back to the police, asking them to apply the correct legal sections before resubmitting it.

The complainant challenged this order before the Peshawar High Court, arguing that the Sessions Judge had no authority to do this. The High Court agreed. It explained that under the Criminal Procedure Code, once a case triable exclusively by the Sessions Court is forwarded to it, the judge's job at this stage is limited to reviewing the police report, documents, and statements to decide whether there are grounds to frame a charge and proceed with trial. The law does not give a Sessions Court the power to declare an FIR's registration doubtful without evidence, nor to send the case back to the police for correcting the charged offence.

The High Court therefore quashed the Sessions Judge's order and directed him to proceed with the case following the proper trial procedure. This judgment matters because it clarifies the limits of a Sessions Court's authority at the pre-charge stage and reinforces that courts must follow the specific procedural steps laid down in the law rather than short-circuiting the process.

title: Powers of High Court are wide under 561-A of CRPC
explainer:
This case from the Sindh High Court dealt with a criminal case arising from a fight at a hotel in Karachi in 2002. The applicant, Muhammad Hanif, was accused in an FIR of attacking a person named Sajid with a knife (churri), causing him serious injury, along with several co-accused armed with sticks and rods.

However, before this FIR was registered, an earlier police report about the same incident described a much less serious assault by different attackers using no weapons, and made no mention of Hanif or a knife. When the case went to trial, the medical officer who examined the victim testified that all his injuries were caused by a blunt object, not a sharp weapon, and could even have been self-inflicted. This directly contradicted the FIR's story.

Based on this, Hanif asked the trial court to acquit him early under Section 265-K of the Criminal Procedure Code, but the trial judge refused, saying the evidence still showed his involvement. Hanif then approached the High Court.

The High Court held that its inherent powers under Section 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code are very wide and exist to prevent misuse of the judicial process and secure real justice. Given the contradictions in the prosecution's own evidence, Hanif's age, ill health, and the lack of any real chance of conviction, the Court found the continuing prosecution to be an abuse of process and quashed the case against him. The judgment illustrates how courts can step in to stop clearly baseless prosecutions from continuing.

title: Promotion of Civil Servants Case Law
explainer:
Here's a plain-language explainer of this Supreme Court judgment.

This case dealt with the promotion of senior civil servants (in grade BPS-20, from the Pakistan Administrative Service, Police Service, and Foreign Service) to the higher grade of BPS-21. A Central Selection Board had recommended a group of officers for promotion, but the Prime Minister's office sent back the recommendations concerning some of these officers for reconsideration rather than approving them. Those officers went to the Islamabad High Court and the Lahore High Court, both of which ruled in their favor, holding that the Board's recommendations were largely binding and could only be returned in cases of clear procedural or legal flaws, and that singling out these officers while approving others amounted to discrimination.

title: Discrimination is not allowed to any Pakistani under Article 25
explainer:
This case dealt with alleged discrimination in the recruitment of Primary Teaching Certificate (PTC) teachers in NWFP (now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa). The Education Department had advertised PTC teaching posts with a condition that candidates who qualified from Elementary Colleges within NWFP would get preference over those who obtained the same qualification from other recognized institutions, such as Allama Iqbal Open University or institutions in Sindh. The petitioners, who held valid PTC qualifications from such other institutions, were denied consideration because of this preference and challenged it as unconstitutional.

The Peshawar High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners, holding that this preferential treatment violated Article 25 of the Constitution, which guarantees equality of citizens and prohibits discrimination. The court noted that once an institution's qualification is officially recognized by the government and the University Grants Commission, it must be treated equally with other recognized qualifications. It found no logical or legal basis for favoring NWFP-based PTC graduates, especially since no such preference existed for other teaching posts like Senior English or Vernacular Teachers. The court also rejected the department's justification that NWFP colleges admitted students based on district vacancies, calling it irrelevant and not linked to merit.

This judgment is significant because it reinforces that government recruitment policies cannot arbitrarily favor one recognized institution's graduates over another's, and that equal treatment of qualified citizens under Article 25 must guide public employment decisions.

title: Power of Attorney must be valid for filing Ejectment Petition
explainer:
This case involved eviction proceedings filed by Habib Bank Limited against three tenants (Crescent Jute Products and two others) occupying bank premises in Faisalabad. The tenants challenged the eviction petitions on the ground that the bank official who filed them was not properly authorized to do so on the bank's behalf.

The Special Judge (Rent) initially agreed with the tenants and dismissed the eviction petitions as improperly filed. However, an Additional District Judge reversed this on appeal, accepting the bank's power of attorney document as valid and ordering the tenants' eviction.

The Lahore High Court examined the document, called an Officer's Power of Attorney, and found it to be a generic, pre-printed form used across the bank's branches, with blanks filled in for the relevant officer's name. Crucially, it was not backed by any specific resolution of the bank's Board of Directors authorizing that individual to initiate legal proceedings, and it had not been registered as required under the Registration Act and Stamp Act. The court held that such documents must be strictly construed, and no authority can be assumed beyond what is explicitly stated in them.

Relying on earlier Supreme Court rulings, the High Court ruled that a company or bank must execute a specific, properly authorized power of attorney for each legal proceeding. Administrative convenience cannot override this legal requirement. The court therefore restored the original decision, holding that the eviction petitions were filed by an unauthorized person and were legally invalid.

title: Vehicle Forgery Quashment Judgment
explainer:
This case involved a car that was seized by police in 2010 after its chassis number was found to be tampered with and its registration documents turned out to be forged. The trial court had ordered the vehicle confiscated to the State, even though the people involved in the alleged forgery and sale were acquitted of criminal charges, and no appeal was filed against those acquittals. The vehicle's possessor, Muhammad Qasim, and his son approached the Peshawar High Court asking that the confiscation order be cancelled and the car returned to them.

The High Court ruled in their favor. It noted that since no one was actually convicted of forgery, and there was no proof of guilty intent (mens rea) on the part of the petitioners, they could not be penalized by losing their vehicle. The court emphasized that Qasim and his family were the only claimants and long-term possessors of the car, and in the case of movable property, possession itself is strong evidence of ownership. No rival owner had come forward in three years, and there was no evidence the car was stolen.

The court held that a defect in paperwork or a tampered chassis number does not justify confiscating a vehicle from an innocent, bona fide owner. Instead, such defects should be corrected through the proper legal process under motor vehicle registration law, including payment of applicable fees. The confiscation order was quashed, and the car was ordered returned once properly re-registered.

title: Commission of Cognizable Offence is sufficient for registration of FIR
explainer:
This case is about a challenge to police guidelines for investigating cheque fraud cases under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with dishonestly issuing a cheque that bounces. The Inspector General of Punjab Police had issued instructions requiring three things before an FIR (First Information Report) could be registered: a dishonour slip, a notice under Section 30 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, and proof of dishonesty and genuineness of the accused's signature. The petitioner argued these conditions amounted to an unlawful pre-FIR inquiry, since the law only requires that a complaint disclose a cognizable offence for police to register a case.

The Lahore High Court agreed in part. It ruled that requiring a dishonour slip and legal notice before registering an FIR was valid, since these simply confirm that an offence appears to have occurred. However, requiring police to verify dishonesty and signature authenticity before registration was improper, since these are matters for investigation and evidence, not a precondition for filing the FIR. The court clarified that this last requirement could still be examined afterward, before arresting the accused.

The judgment also emphasized that arrest is not automatic upon FIR registration; it should only happen once there's sufficient evidence, protecting people from being detained on unproven allegations. This matters because it balances efficient law enforcement with protecting individual liberty from premature arrest.

title: Tenancy can be inherited under section 19-A
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over agricultural land in Punjab that Lal Din bought at auction in 1941 under a colonial-era land law, dying in 1945 and leaving behind a widow, five sons, and five daughters. After his death, the sons had the land recorded in their names, paid off the remaining installments, and eventually became owners in 1956. Decades later, in 1998, one daughter sued claiming her Islamic inheritance share, arguing she was entitled to part of the property as Lal Din's legal heir.

Lower courts and the High Court sided with the daughter, reasoning that since ownership was formally transferred in 1956, after a 1951 amendment (Section 19-A) made such tenancy rights inheritable under Muslim law, she should get her share.

The Supreme Court disagreed and allowed the appeal. It clarified that what mattered legally was the date of the tenant's death, not when ownership documents were later finalized. Since Lal Din died in 1945, before Section 19-A came into force in 1951, his tenancy rights passed according to the older Section 20, which limited inheritance to male lineal descendants only. The daughters therefore could not claim a share under either Section 19-A or the Muslim Personal Law Application Act.

This case matters because it clarifies how changes in inheritance law apply based on the date of death, not the date administrative paperwork is completed, affecting property rights in older land disputes.

title: Property can be attached during execution of Decree
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the sale of a Toyota Corolla car. The buyer had paid a partial amount and taken possession of the vehicle, while the seller kept the registration documents and was owed the remaining balance, guaranteed by a third-party surety. When the buyer failed to pay, the seller sued for the outstanding amount and won an uncontested (ex-parte) decree ordering payment.

During execution of this decree, the decree-holder got the police to seize the car from a person who was neither the original buyer nor a party to the case, claiming this person was a bona fide purchaser and last possessor of the vehicle. That person challenged the seizure. The trial court, without following proper legal procedure, effectively ordered the vehicle confiscated.

The Balochistan High Court found this improper. It held that a court executing a decree cannot go beyond what the decree actually says, and must follow the specific legal procedures under the Civil Procedure Code before attaching or selling any property to satisfy a decree. Crucially, no formal order of attachment had ever been issued for the vehicle, and there was no proof the vehicle was being held by anyone on behalf of the original judgment debtors. Simply having police seize the car did not amount to a lawful attachment.

The court ruled that the vehicle's possession must be restored to the appellant, since the improper seizure had no legal effect. This case reinforces that courts must strictly follow proper legal procedure when attaching property during decree execution, protecting the rights of third parties not involved in the original judgment.

title: Judgment in a case under Cantonments Act, 1925
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Rawalpindi. Zafar Iqbal owned a house and was served notice by the Cantonment Board to dismantle certain allegedly illegal constructions. He filed a civil suit seeking a permanent injunction to stop the Board from demolishing his house, gate, boundary walls, or using his land as a passage for others.

During the trial, a retired army officer, Subedar Muhammad Khan, applied to join the case as a party, arguing that Zafar Iqbal had blocked a street he and others used, and that the outcome of the suit would affect his rights. The trial court allowed him to be added as a necessary party, and this decision was upheld on appeal by the Additional District Judge. Zafar Iqbal then challenged both rulings before the Lahore High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that Muhammad Khan was not just acting as a public-spirited outsider but had a genuine personal stake in the dispute, since he was already involved in related litigation over the same street. The court explained that decisions about adding parties to a lawsuit fall within the trial court's discretion, and higher courts should not interfere with that discretion unless it leads to a clear miscarriage of justice. Since both lower courts had reasonably found Muhammad Khan's presence necessary for fully resolving the dispute, there was no valid ground to overturn their orders. The petition was therefore rejected.

title: Consent decree is not applicable on those who are not party in a case
explainer:
This case is about a long-running land dispute over Shamlat Deh land in Kaskalyal village, Mirpur, and whether a decree agreed to by some people could bind others who were never made part of the lawsuit.

The dispute began with a consent decree passed in 1990, based on an agreement between certain parties, concerning land in the village. Later, other parties who claimed ownership and possession of the same land, but who had never been included as defendants in that earlier case, challenged the decree and a related ex-parte decree. The trial court eventually set aside the 1998 ex-parte decree after hearing evidence, prompting the losing side to file this revision petition before the Azad Jammu and Kashmir High Court.

The High Court examined the history of the litigation and the fact that the petitioners, who were in actual possession of the land, had never been made parties to the earlier proceedings even though they were necessary parties. The Court held that a consent decree cannot bind persons who were not parties to that case. It further held that once such a decree is not legally in effect, any sale deed executed on its basis is also legally non-existent. Finding that the trial court had correctly appreciated the evidence and applied the law, the High Court accepted the revision petition and upheld the trial court's order.

The judgment matters because it reinforces the basic principle that court decisions and settlements can only bind the actual parties involved, protecting the rights of those left out of litigation affecting their property.

title: Application to make legal heirs party to the suit
explainer:
This case involved a decades-long legal dispute that began in 1975, when Jameel Ahmed sued Saifuddin seeking a declaration that Saifuddin had unlawfully revoked a general power of attorney he had earlier given to Ahmed over a Karachi business. Because Saifuddin was an Indian national unable to travel to Pakistan, he could not appear, and an ex-parte decree was passed against him. After appeals and a earlier High Court revision, the case was sent back to the trial court in 1984 for further proceedings, but it remained undecided for another decade. Saifuddin died in 1994, and his legal heirs applied to be substituted as defendants under Order 22 Rule 4 of the Civil Procedure Code. The trial court dismissed this application, reasoning that since Saifuddin never filed a written statement, his heirs had no real right to be formally added as parties, only to cross-examine witnesses.

The Sindh High Court overturned this decision. It held that legal heirs are entitled to step into the shoes of a deceased litigant, and refusing to add them denies natural justice. The court found no valid reason, including delay, to justify blocking their substitution, especially since the other side had not raised the delay issue earlier and suffered no prejudice. The judgment clarifies that courts should not use technicalities to deny heirs their rightful place in ongoing litigation, ensuring fair representation continues even after a party's death.

title: Parties are bound to follow terms of Employment Agreement
explainer:
This case involved six young doctors employed on contract at a government hospital in Landi Kotal, in what was then the NWFP province. Their services were terminated suddenly by government order in August 2000, on the ground that they had been absent from duty. They had received no prior charge, warning, inquiry, or show-cause notice before being dismissed. The doctors challenged this termination in the Peshawar High Court, arguing it violated their employment agreement and basic fairness, since they were essentially condemned without being heard.

The government argued the doctors, being contract employees rather than regular civil servants, had no right to approach the High Court and should instead file a civil suit.

The court disagreed with the government and ruled in favor of the doctors. It held that although the government could freely terminate a simple contract without giving reasons, once it chose to terminate on the specific ground of misconduct (absence from duty), it was bound by the procedure set out in the employment agreement itself, which required following the NWFP Efficiency and Discipline Rules. The government could not dictate contract terms and then ignore them when convenient. Since no proper inquiry or evidence was produced, and the termination stigmatized the doctors' careers, the court found the order unlawful and ordered their reinstatement.

The case matters because it establishes that contractual employees are entitled to fair procedure when accused of misconduct, and that employers are equally bound by the terms of contracts they draft.

title: Grant of Bail is a rule when punishment is less than 10 years
explainer:
This case is about M. Aslam, who was accused of issuing a cheque worth Rs. 90,38,000 that later bounced when presented at the bank, an offence under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code (dishonour of cheque). He was arrested and sought bail from the Lahore High Court.

The petitioner argued the FIR was filed with mala fide intent, noting a two-year unexplained delay in reporting the matter, no mention of witnesses, date, time or place of the alleged transaction, and that he actually had documents showing he purchased land from the complainant, paying Rs. 15,00,000, with the cheque meant only as a guarantee for a smaller remaining amount that was allegedly altered by the complainant. He also pointed to a separate FIR his brother had filed against the complainant alleging forgery of the same cheque.

The court noted that the maximum punishment for the offence under Section 489-F is only three years, meaning the case does not fall under the more serious category of offences where bail is restricted. Relying on Supreme Court precedent (PLD 1995 SC 34), the judge explained that for offences carrying less than ten years imprisonment, granting bail is the norm and refusal the exception, unless there is risk of the accused fleeing, tampering with evidence, repeating the offense, or being a previous convict.

Given the delay, weak evidence, and disputed facts, the court found grounds to grant bail to the petitioner.

title: A person who runs from law loses some of his rights
explainer:
This case concerns a man named Karam Illahi who was accused of fraud. A complainant alleged that Illahi took Rs. 200,000 from him with a false promise of arranging emigration abroad, then failed to deliver and refused to refund the money, eventually issuing a cheque that bounced. Based on this, a criminal case was registered against him under laws covering dishonoured cheques and emigration fraud.

Instead of facing the case, Illahi asked the Peshawar High Court to quash the FIR (the police complaint) against him using its special inherent powers. However, before the court could even consider the merits of his request, the State's lawyer raised an objection: Illahi had already been declared a fugitive, since a magistrate had issued arrest warrants against him which he was actively avoiding, leading to proceedings to attach his property.

The High Court agreed with this objection and refused to hear his petition at all. It relied on earlier rulings from Pakistan's Supreme Court and High Courts establishing a clear principle: someone who evades the legal process and refuses to surrender to arrest warrants cannot simultaneously ask the courts for relief. Courts will not assist a person who is dodging justice.

This case matters because it reinforces an important rule of fairness in the justice system: people cannot pick and choose when to engage with the law. If you flee from lawful arrest, you temporarily forfeit your right to ask courts for favorable outcomes until you first submit to the legal process.

title: Can the property be attached in a recovery of dower suit?
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over whether a house could be seized to satisfy a court judgment. Muhammad Hafeez had acted as a surety (guarantor) for someone who owed Rs. 12,50,000 under a court decree. When the debtor failed to pay, the court ordered attachment of a property Hafeez had listed as his own in the surety bond. However, Hafeez's wife, Tasawar Yaseen, objected, arguing that this same property had actually been given to her by her husband at the time of their nikah (marriage contract) as part of arrangements recorded in the nikah nama, meaning it belonged to her, not her husband, and therefore could not be attached to pay his debt.

The trial court's executing court rejected her objection and allowed the attachment to proceed. She appealed to the Lahore High Court.

The High Court sided with the wife. It found that the nikah nama clearly recorded that the husband had given her the property and had agreed to formally transfer his share to her on demand. The court held that such an entry in a nikah nama is itself sufficient legal proof of a property transfer, without needing separate registration or documentation. Since the husband had already relinquished his rights over the property before offering it as surety, he had no authority to pledge it. The court also found suspicious a power-of-attorney document produced by the other side, which appeared to be fraudulently prepared.

As a result, the attachment order was set aside, and the wife's objection was upheld. The case matters because it confirms that property rights transferred through a nikah nama are legally protected, even against creditors of

title: Can the property be attached during trial?
explainer:
This case is about whether a court order attaching a defendant's property during an ongoing lawsuit remains valid after the lawsuit itself is dismissed, even while an appeal against that dismissal is pending.

A recovery suit for over Rs. 41 lakh was filed against Muhammad Imran Tehseen and others. During the trial, the plaintiffs asked the court to attach the defendants' property or require them to furnish a bank guarantee, to prevent them from disposing of assets before a possible decree. The trial court granted this request. Separately, one defendant asked to be removed from the case, claiming he had been wrongly included, but this request was rejected. Both orders were challenged before the Balochistan High Court through revision petitions.

While the petitions were pending, the trial court dismissed the main suit, and an appeal against that dismissal was filed and remained pending elsewhere.

The High Court held that under the Code of Civil Procedure, an attachment made before judgment automatically ends once the suit is dismissed, whether or not the trial court explicitly says so. The pendency of an appeal against the dismissal does not revive the attachment. Even if the appellate court later overturns the dismissal and sends the case back for further proceedings, the original attachment order still does not automatically come back into effect. On this basis, the petitions were dismissed as no longer having practical relevance.

This ruling clarifies that provisional measures like property attachment are tied strictly to the life of the suit and lapse automatically upon its dismissal.

title: Talaq can be revoked within 90 days
explainer:
This case is about whether a husband could cancel a divorce (talaq) he had pronounced against his wife, before the process under Pakistan's Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 was completed.

The petitioner divorced his wife in December 2010 and notified the Arbitration Council, as required by law. The Council began proceedings to confirm the divorce and attempt reconciliation. Before the 90-day period required under Section 7 of the Ordinance expired, the husband sent a letter withdrawing his notice of divorce. Despite this, the Council continued asking him to confirm whether the divorce still stood, prompting him to go to the Sindh High Court.

The wife argued the divorce had already become final, especially given a history of litigation between the couple, a public notice of divorce, and affidavits confirming it. She said there was no legal provision allowing withdrawal of talaq.

The High Court disagreed. It held that under Section 7(3) of the Ordinance, a talaq can be revoked, either expressly or through conduct, as long as this happens within 90 days from when the Chairman of the Arbitration Council receives notice of the divorce. Since the husband revoked his divorce notice within that window, the Arbitration Council no longer had authority to proceed further, either to confirm the divorce or attempt reconciliation.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that the 90-day period is not just a waiting period before divorce becomes final, but a genuine window during which a husband can lawfully cancel the divorce, after which authorities must stop all further

title: Only husband can pronounce Talaq
explainer:
This case involved a woman, Ruqia Bano, who sought a court declaration (jactitation of marriage) that she was not the legally wedded wife of a man named Mureed Hussain. She claimed she was abducted and forced to give thumb impressions on documents, and that she remained the wife of her original husband, Qurban Hussain. Mureed Hussain, on the other hand, claimed she had been divorced by Qurban Hussain and had then validly married him, and he filed a separate suit demanding restitution of conjugal rights.

The Family Court and the Appellate Court both ruled against Ruqia Bano, accepting that she had been divorced and was validly married to Mureed Hussain, based largely on her own earlier statement that she had been divorced.

The Lahore High Court overturned these decisions. It held that under the law, divorce (talaq) must be pronounced by the husband himself, and a wife's mere statement claiming she was divorced is not sufficient proof, especially since the alleged written divorce document was never produced as evidence. The court found the lower courts had misread the evidence and wrongly presumed a divorce had occurred simply because the wife claimed it had.

This matters because it clarifies an important legal principle: divorce cannot be assumed from a wife's statement alone, and courts must have real evidence of the husband actually pronouncing it. The petition was allowed, the divorce suit for jactitation of marriage was granted, and the conjugal rights claim was dismissed.

title: Wife is entitled for maintainance even without rukhsati
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a husband and wife over money claims arising from their marriage. The wife had filed a suit seeking maintenance allowance, dower (mehr), and an additional amount that the nikahnama stated would become payable to her if she was divorced. The Appellate Court had granted her only the maintenance allowance, rejecting the other claims, and both spouses challenged this outcome before the Lahore High Court through a constitutional petition.

The High Court upheld the Appellate Court's decision. It ruled that the Family Court did not have jurisdiction to hear the wife's claim for the extra conditional amount tied to divorce as written in the nikahnama. Her claim for dower also failed because the nikahnama itself recorded that the dower had already been paid to her at the time of the marriage ceremony, and she had admitted in cross-examination that she never challenged this entry anywhere.

On the maintenance issue, the court rejected the husband's argument that she was not entitled to any maintenance. It held that a valid Nikah under Islamic law itself creates the wife's right to maintenance, even before rukhsati (the sending of the bride to the husband's home), as long as she remains willing to fulfill her marital obligations. Since the evidence showed the wife never refused to join her husband and it was actually the husband who delayed rukhsati and eventually divorced her, she was rightly entitled to maintenance from the date of nikah until divorce, plus the iddat period. The petition was dismissed.

title: Case of Prompt Dower
explainer:
This case is about a wife, Shamshad Bibi, who filed a lawsuit seeking both maintenance (financial support) and her prompt dower, which had been fixed in her marriage contract (nikahnama) as gold ornaments worth Rs. 30,000, or their equivalent cash value.

The Family Court had already granted her the dower but rejected her claim for maintenance. When she appealed, the Appellate Court upheld that decision, so she approached the High Court under its constitutional writ jurisdiction.

The High Court explained an important principle of Muslim family law: when a wife has not been paid her prompt dower, she has the legal right to refuse to live with her husband until it is paid, and during that period he remains responsible for her maintenance. The Court held that simply filing the lawsuit for dower counted as formally demanding it, so the husband's duty to pay maintenance began from the date the suit was filed and continued until the dower was actually paid.

Since the husband had not challenged the dower decree itself, and had not disclosed his income despite working in Saudi Arabia (while the wife claimed he earned Rs. 40,000-50,000 per month), the Court found the earlier maintenance amount inadequate. It fixed maintenance at Rs. 1,000 per month, payable from the date of the suit until the dower was paid, and modified the lower courts' decisions accordingly.

This case matters because it clarifies wives' rights regarding unpaid dower and the linked entitlement to maintenance during the period of non-payment.

title: Petition of leave to Appeal
explainer:
This case involved two government employees who challenged a High Court judgment that had dismissed their writ petitions. Instead of filing the correct legal remedy, an Intra Court Appeal before the High Court, they mistakenly filed petitions for leave to appeal directly to the Supreme Court.

The Federation argued that since the law provided for an Intra Court Appeal against such judgments, these petitions for leave to appeal were not the proper remedy and should simply be dismissed, leaving the petitioners to file fresh Intra Court Appeals.

The Supreme Court noted that one petitioner had filed within 20 days of the judgment, meaning an Intra Court Appeal would still be within time, while the other had filed on the 58th day, which would make a fresh appeal potentially time-barred. The Court found that the petitioners had made an honest mistake, likely due to wrong legal advice, and that simply dismissing their petitions and forcing them to start over would be an unnecessary technical exercise.

Rather than penalize the petitioners for this procedural error, the Supreme Court decided to convert their petitions into Intra Court Appeals and sent them back to the High Court to be decided on merits, with the High Court to separately examine any limitation issues.

This judgment matters because it shows courts can look past procedural technicalities and relabel a case correctly to ensure people get a fair hearing, rather than losing their case purely due to a filing mistake.

title: Husband cannot skip maintenance of child
explainer:
This case is about a father who tried to avoid paying maintenance for his child by claiming the child was illegitimate. The father argued that the child was born about 11 months after he and his wife had separated, and used this timing to suggest the child was not his.

Both the Family Court and the Appellate Court had already ordered him to pay monthly maintenance for the minor child, and he challenged this by filing a constitutional petition in the Lahore High Court.

The High Court rejected the father's argument. It held that under Islamic law, a child born to a married woman is presumed to be legitimate, and this presumption stands unless there is strong, credible proof to the contrary. Simply alleging that the wife had an affair or disowning the child was not enough. The court noted that the father had not taken the proper legal route of seeking Li'an (a formal Islamic procedure for a husband to deny paternity), which further weakened his case. Since there was no solid evidence proving the child was illegitimate, the child was legally presumed to be the father's own and therefore entitled to maintenance.

The court dismissed the father's petition and upheld the maintenance order. This case matters because it reinforces that fathers cannot easily deny responsibility for a child born during marriage, protecting children's rights to support and legitimacy in the absence of solid proof otherwise.

title: When principle of double jeopardy can be invoked
explainer:
This case, decided by the Supreme Court of Pakistan, dealt with whether accused persons who had earlier been left out of a police charge sheet (and thus not sent for trial) could later be summoned by the trial court to face charges, or whether doing so would violate the principle of double jeopardy, which protects a person from being tried or punished twice for the same offence.

The case arose from a 1999 murder FIR in which police, after investigation, charged only two of several named accused. The complainant later applied under Section 193 of the Criminal Procedure Code to have the remaining accused summoned as well. After years of litigation, the trial court reviewed evidence and decided there was enough material to summon the additional accused. The High Court upheld this decision, and the accused challenged it before the Supreme Court, arguing they had effectively been cleared during investigation and that being summoned now amounted to being tried twice.

The Supreme Court rejected this argument. It held that being excluded from a police report or discharged at the investigation stage is not the same as an acquittal by a court, and does not bind the trial court's independent assessment of evidence. Since the accused had never actually been tried or acquitted, there was no double jeopardy. The Court found the trial court's decision to summon them was a reasonable, evidence-based judgment, not arbitrary, and dismissed the petition, allowing the trial to proceed.

title: Nawaz Sharif Benami Helicopter Case
explainer:

The allegation was that in 1993 he purchased a Russian MI-8 helicopter, used it for his election campaign, and spent large sums on leasing, buying, and maintaining it that could not be explained by his declared income. It was also alleged he used an associate, Saif-ur-Rehman, to disguise the purchase as belonging to someone else to avoid paying taxes. He was originally sentenced to 14 years in prison, a heavy fine, and a 21-year disqualification from holding public office.

On appeal, the Lahore High Court (Rawalpindi Bench) overturned the conviction and acquitted him of all charges. The court found that the prosecution presented no real evidence linking Nawaz Sharif to payments for the helicopter's lease, purchase, or upkeep. The court also found serious procedural problems: the trial court wrongly allowed a legal presumption of guilt to be applied against him without meeting the legal conditions for it, permitted improper re-examination of a witness, and admitted unproven documents. title: Confession made by accused in police custody is irrelevant
explainer:
This case involved Karamat Ali, a driver at WAPDA (the Water and Power Development Authority), who was dismissed from service over accusations that he stole generator winding bars from a store. The Federal Service Tribunal had earlier ordered fresh inquiry proceedings against him, but he was dismissed again after that inquiry, prompting him to appeal a second time.

The key issue was the evidence used against him. The most important potential witness, a scrap dealer from whose house the stolen items were recovered, was never questioned or had his statement recorded. Instead, the department relied heavily on a confession the appellant allegedly made while he was in police custody.

The Tribunal ruled that such a confession could not be used against him, citing Article 39 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, which says confessions made while in police custody are not legally relevant. Although this rule is mainly meant for criminal cases, the Tribunal held that the same principle should apply in disciplinary proceedings, especially since there was no other real evidence against him.

Because the crucial witness was never examined, the Tribunal found the inquiry was not conducted properly. It set aside the dismissal, reinstated the appellant, and ordered a fresh inquiry that must include recording the scrap dealer's statement. Back pay would depend on the outcome of this new inquiry.

The case highlights that confessions extracted while someone is in police custody cannot be treated as reliable evidence, even in workplace disciplinary matters.

title: Wife is not liable to return dower in all khula cases
explainer:
This Sindh High Court judgment deals with a dispute over "khula", a wife's right to seek divorce from her husband through the courts even without his consent, on the ground that she cannot continue the marriage within limits set by Islam.

The wife had sued for dissolution of her marriage, alleging cruelty and mistreatment by her husband. The Family Court granted her divorce through khula but did not order her to return her dower (mehr) to the husband, reasoning that giving back the dower is not a mandatory condition for granting khula. The husband challenged this decision in the High Court, arguing that khula could not be granted unless the dower was returned to him.

The High Court rejected the husband's argument. It held that returning dower is not compulsory for a khula decree to be valid; whether mutual benefits like dower should be restored depends on the facts of each case and only creates a separate civil obligation, not a condition for the divorce itself. The court noted the wife had lived with her husband for over a year and a half, which could be seen as sufficient benefit to him, and that she came from a poor background and had already endured lengthy litigation. The court also ruled that since a decision on restoring dower can be appealed under the Family Courts law, the husband should have filed an appeal instead of going directly to the High Court, making his petition not maintainable.

This case matters because it protects women, especially poor women, from being trapped in unwanted marriages simply because they cannot afford to repay dower or other benefits received during the marriage.

title: Value of defective power of attorney document
explainer:
This case involved a woman who filed a lawsuit for dissolution of her marriage before the Family Court in Lahore. She filed the case through a special attorney using a power of attorney document. The Family Court judge dismissed her suit because the power of attorney had problems: it was written on plain paper instead of proper stamp paper, and it had not been verified by an Oath Commissioner as required by law. The judge also had doubts about whether the signature on the document was genuine. Since the woman herself had never appeared in court and the document authorizing her attorney to act on her behalf was legally defective, the judge threw out her case.

She then challenged this dismissal before the Lahore High Court. Her lawyer pointed out that she was now present in court in person and was willing to appear before the Family Court herself to fix the problem.

The High Court agreed that such defects in a power of attorney are not fatal to a case. They can be corrected simply by having the person appear in court personally and confirm, through her own statement, that she had indeed authorized the attorney to act for her. Based on this, the High Court sent the case back to the Family Court, directing that she appear in person to resolve the issue, and ordered the trial to be completed within 60 days.

This decision matters because it shows that minor procedural or documentation errors should not automatically defeat a person's right to have their case heard, especially in family matters, as long as the defect can be cured through proper court appearance.

title: Order 16 Rule 1 CPC : Summoning of Witnesses Application dismissed
explainer:
This case is about a lawsuit for pre-emption, where a person claiming a superior right to buy land tried to prove he had properly given legal notice of his intention to purchase. Under the Civil Procedure Code, parties to a lawsuit must submit a list of witnesses within seven days of the court framing the issues in the case. The plaintiff failed to do this. After his own witnesses had already testified, he suddenly applied, at a very late stage, to have the postman summoned as a witness to prove that the notice had been sent by registered post.

Both the trial court and the appellate court (Additional District Judge) rejected this request, holding that he had not shown any good or sufficient reason for failing to list this witness earlier, and that allowing it would let him patch up gaps in his evidence rather than prove his case properly from the start.

The High Court agreed with the lower courts. It explained that while courts do have discretion to allow a late witness even if not originally listed, this discretion can only be used if the party shows good and sufficient cause for the delay. Since the plaintiff offered no valid explanation and seemed to be trying to fix weaknesses in his case after the fact, the courts below were right to refuse his request. The petition was dismissed.

The case highlights how strictly procedural deadlines for listing witnesses are enforced in civil litigation, especially in pre-emption suits.

title: Muhammad Afaq Shamsi Versus National Accountability Bureau
explainer:
This case involved directors and guarantors of Quice Food Industries Limited, a company that had defaulted on a bank loan. The bank had won a court decree against the company and later agreed to restructure the debt, allowing repayment in instalments under a new agreement. The execution of the original decree was put on hold while the company paid according to this new arrangement, and the bank confirmed the account was being paid regularly.

Meanwhile, the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) had filed a corruption reference against the company directors for wilful default on the loan. The accused sought to have the case dismissed, arguing that since the debt was being repaid under the new agreement, there was no wilful default. The Accountability Court refused, saying the matter needed evidence and trial.

The Sindh High Court disagreed. It held that the new repayment agreement legally replaced the original loan agreement, a concept called novation under the Contract Act. Since the old obligations were extinguished and replaced by new ones, any default would have to be judged against the new agreement, not the old one. As payments were being made regularly under the new deal, there was no wilful default. NAB's argument that payment must go directly to it, not the bank, was also rejected. The court stayed the criminal proceedings and ordered them quashed if full payment was completed, while allowing NAB to revive the case if a genuine default occurred later.

title: Kohinoor Mills Versus SECP
explainer:
Kohinoor Spinning Mills Ltd. approached the Lahore High Court seeking confirmation of a special resolution to reduce its share capital by 50 percent, from Rs 10 to Rs 5 per share, to offset accumulated losses of over Rs 916 million caused by high financial costs and operating losses. The company had followed the legal procedure under the Companies Ordinance, 1984, including notifying shareholders and secured creditors and publishing notices in newspapers. No shareholder or creditor objected. The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) appeared but raised an objection that the Lahore High Court lacked territorial jurisdiction because the company was registered with an Islamabad office.

The court rejected this objection. It held that under the Companies Ordinance, the High Court with jurisdiction is the one where the company's registered office is located. Since Kohinoor's registered office was in Chakwal, which falls within the Lahore High Court's territorial jurisdiction, the court had authority to hear the matter regardless of any Islamabad registration reference.

Finding all legal requirements met and no genuine opposition, the court disposed of the petition, effectively allowing the capital reduction to proceed.

This case matters because it clarifies that jurisdiction in company law matters follows the location of a company's registered office, not other administrative addresses, providing useful guidance for future corporate restructuring cases.

title: Judgment on Disowning child by the father
explainer:
This case, decided by the Lahore High Court, dealt with a dispute over the legitimacy of a child. The child's mother had filed a maintenance suit on behalf of herself and her minor son against the father, who denied that the child was his and refused to support him. The father asked the Family Court to order a DNA test to prove the child was not his, but the Family Court rejected this request. He then challenged that refusal before the High Court.

The High Court upheld the Family Court's decision and dismissed the father's petition at the outset. It held that questions of a child's legitimacy have serious, lasting consequences and cannot be decided casually. Under the law, a child born during a lawful marriage is presumed legitimate, and this presumption strongly favors the child. A father cannot simply deny paternity through bare accusations; such claims must be backed by solid, credible evidence. The court noted that the father had not pursued the proper legal procedure (called "Liyan") available for formally disowning a child, nor had he presented any real proof that the child was illegitimate.

Because the child was born during the marriage and no credible evidence rebutted the presumption of legitimacy, the court ruled that the child was legitimate and was legally entitled to receive maintenance from the father. This case highlights how strongly the law protects children born in wedlock from being denied support based on unsubstantiated claims.
