title: Judgment against qadianis in Pakistan
explainer:
This case involved two brothers from Mansehra who belonged to the Ahmadi (Qadiani) community and were charged under sections 298-B and 298-C of the Pakistan Penal Code, which make it a criminal offence for Ahmadis to "profess" Islam or use Islamic terms and practices reserved for Muslims. These sections were added through a 1984 ordinance dealing with anti-Islamic activities of Qadianis and Ahmadis.

The complaint against the two men was that, when filling out Form A to obtain their National Identity Cards, they had listed their religion as Islam. However, the court noted a crucial timing problem: the form had been filled out in August 1982, while the law criminalizing an Ahmadi professing Islam only came into force in April 1984. So at the time they filled the form, no such offence existed.

Moreover, evidence at trial showed the men had consistently identified as Ahmadi, including in later official documents registering their children, and never claimed to be Muslim after the law came into effect.

The Peshawar High Court ruled that prosecuting them was both legally baseless and a clear abuse of the court process, since the alleged act did not constitute a crime when it occurred, and violated their constitutional right to religious freedom. The court quashed the case entirely and acquitted both men, ordering their bail bonds discharged.

title: Ingredients of 489-F are important in Check Dishonor Case
explainer:
This case involved a bail petition before the Lahore High Court in a cheque dishonor case under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, which criminalizes issuing a cheque that later bounces when there was dishonest intention behind it.

The petitioner, Muhammad Jameel, had been accused of issuing a cheque worth over six hundred thousand rupees that could not be cashed. He was arrested and sought post-arrest bail. His lawyer argued that the petitioner and the complainant had an ongoing business relationship as buyer and seller of diesel and petrol, that accounts between them were disputed and unsettled, and that this was really a matter requiring rendition of accounts rather than a clear-cut criminal offense.

The court examined the facts and found genuine ambiguity. The complainant himself admitted in court that there was an unresolved issue involving rent for a car that had been in the petitioner's possession, and an adjustment of money related to that rent, none of which had been mentioned in the original police report. The petitioner also had not specified exact dates of credit transactions or when debts were settled.

Given these unresolved factual disputes, the court held that the essential ingredients of the Section 489-F offense were not clearly established, and the case warranted further inquiry rather than continued detention. Bail was granted upon furnishing surety bonds. This case matters because it illustrates how courts distinguish genuine criminal cheque fraud from civil business disputes over accounts.

title: Illegitimate child is state responsibility
explainer:
This case concerns a husband, Waqar Ahmad, who challenged court decisions ordering him to pay dower (mahr) and maintenance to his wife, Nomina Akhtar, and to support their son. The Family Court and an Appellate Court had both ruled against him, so he approached the Peshawar High Court through a constitutional petition.

The couple's marriage was undisputed, as proven by the Nikah Nama. However, the husband tried to deny the child was his, claiming the baby was born prematurely, only six months after the marriage, and therefore illegitimate. His only evidence was an ultrasound report, which he failed to properly prove in court despite having the opportunity to do so.

The High Court rejected this argument. It explained that under Islamic law, a child is presumed legitimate if born anywhere between six months and two years after marriage. Since the husband offered no solid legal proof to rebut this presumption, the child had to be treated as legitimate.

The Court also invoked Article 35 of the Constitution, which obligates the State to protect marriage, family, mothers, and children. It emphasized that wrongly branding a child illegitimate without proper evidence causes severe, lifelong harm, and courts must guard against this injustice.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions, confirming the child's legitimacy and the father's duty to maintain him, along with the wife's dower and maintenance claims.

title: Father is more liable to maintain his child
explainer:
This case involved a father's obligation to pay maintenance for his three minor children. The children's mother had filed a claim for maintenance for herself and the children starting from September 1982. The Family Court initially dismissed the case, but the Additional District Judge reversed this and awarded maintenance to the children from the date the case was filed. The children then went to the High Court seeking maintenance going further back, and the High Court agreed, ordering the father to pay maintenance from September 1982 onward, subject to limitation laws.

The father appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that children should not be entitled to past maintenance the way a wife might be, and separately arguing that since the children's maternal grandparents were already supporting them, he should not have to pay.

The Supreme Court rejected both arguments and dismissed the appeal. It held that there was no legal basis to treat children differently from wives when it comes to awarding past maintenance, and that it would actually be unfair to deny children this benefit while allowing it to wives. On the second point, the Court ruled that a father's duty to maintain his own children takes priority over any obligation of grandparents, even if the grandparents had voluntarily been supporting the children. The father's own lawyer conceded this point during arguments.

This judgment is significant because it firmly establishes that a father cannot avoid his primary responsibility to financially support his children by pointing to other relatives who may be helping out, and confirms that children can claim maintenance for past periods, not just from the date a court case is filed.

title: Constitution petition is not maintainable in case of delay
explainer:
This case involved a wife who filed a family court suit seeking dissolution of her marriage, along with maintenance and recovery of dower and dowry items. When reconciliation efforts failed, the Family Court in Multan granted her a divorce on the basis of khula (a wife-initiated dissolution), but ordered her to return Rs. 500 and five tolas of gold that her Nikkah Nama showed she had received as dower at the time of marriage.

More than four years after this order, the wife challenged it in the Lahore High Court, arguing the direction to return the dower was illegal since her husband had never specifically demanded it and her divorce claim was not based solely on khula.

The High Court dismissed her petition, focusing not on the merits of her argument but on the long delay in bringing the case. It held that constitutional petitions under Article 199 are a form of equitable relief, and such relief cannot be claimed by someone who has been careless or negligent in asserting their rights. Since the wife waited four years without adequate explanation, the court found her guilty of "contumacious lethargy" and gross negligence, and refused to hear her case on that ground alone.

This judgment illustrates an important principle: even if someone may have a valid legal grievance, courts can refuse to intervene if the person delays too long in seeking relief, since constitutional remedies require diligence, not just merit.

title: Adjournment under rule 1 of order 17 of CPC
explainer:
This case involved a civil suit filed in 1995 by Mubashir Khan seeking recovery of Rs. 37,00,000 from Javaid Kamran and others. During the trial, the case was transferred between courts multiple times, and issues were repeatedly amended. On 21 June 2001, when the plaintiff's witnesses were not present, the court granted an adjournment on payment of costs and set 25 June 2001 as the "last and final opportunity" for recording evidence. When the plaintiff still failed to produce evidence on that date, the trial court closed his right to present evidence under Order XVII, Rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code and dismissed his suit for lack of proof.

On appeal, the Lahore High Court found that the defendants had not objected to the earlier adjournment request, and settled law says that such unopposed adjournments should be treated as ordinary adjournments under Rule 1, not as punitive closures under Rule 3. The court also rejected the appellant's claim that the hearing date had been changed without notice, since such claims cannot be proven merely through affidavits when official court records enjoy a presumption of correctness.

The High Court set aside the dismissal and allowed the appeal, giving the plaintiff one final chance to produce his full evidence, subject to paying costs. This decision reinforces protections against harsh, technical dismissals of lawsuits when delays are not caused by deliberate misconduct or objected to by the opposing side.

title: Rejection of Nomination Papers of Proclaimed Offender
explainer:
This case involved a candidate, Umar Farooq, whose nomination papers for both a National Assembly seat (NA-99, Faisalabad) and a Punjab Provincial Assembly seat (PP-107) were rejected by returning officers ahead of the 2024 general elections. The rejection was based on several grounds: his absence during scrutiny of papers, mismatched signatures with his CNIC, failure to disclose a pending criminal case in his affidavit, and improper attestation of that affidavit. An Appellate Tribunal had initially restored his nomination papers, but the Lahore High Court reversed that, holding that because the candidate was allegedly an absconder in the criminal case, he could not be allowed to contest elections, even though he had since obtained pre-arrest bail.

The Supreme Court disagreed and allowed his appeals, restoring his candidacy for both seats. It held that attending the scrutiny of nomination papers is optional, not mandatory, under the law, so absence could not justify rejection. It also found no basis for treating him as an absconder disqualified from contesting, noting that even a formally "proclaimed offender" is not barred from standing for election, so someone merely alleged to be an absconder certainly could not be barred either. Failing to mention the criminal case in his affidavit also did not carry any legal penalty like disqualification.

This judgment matters because it clarifies that mere criminal allegations or absconder status, without formal disqualification under the Constitution or Elections Act, cannot be used to bar candidates from contesting

title: Quashing of FIR, mainly on ground that no offence was made out of allegations recorded in FIR
explainer:
This case involved allegations that several employees of the Capital Development Authority (CDA) had been illegally promoted between 2007 and 2013, in violation of service rules. Following a news report on this, the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) conducted an inquiry, concluded that officers had abused their authority in approving these promotions, and registered an FIR against them under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code and the Prevention of Corruption Act, alleging criminal breach of trust and corruption.

The accused challenged the FIR before the Islamabad High Court, arguing that the allegations, even if true, did not amount to a criminal offence. The High Court agreed and quashed the FIR, holding that irregular promotions were, at most, a violation of service rules and misconduct, not criminal breach of trust or corruption under the law. The FIA challenged this decision before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's ruling and dismissed the FIA's petition. It explained that entrusting an officer with the power to approve promotions is not the same as entrusting them with "property," so misusing that power does not meet the legal definition of criminal breach of trust. Misusing administrative powers may be departmental misconduct, but it is not automatically a crime. The Court also criticized the FIA for pursuing meritless litigation and imposed costs.

This judgment matters because it clarifies the boundary between administrative misconduct and criminal liability, preventing routine service-related irregularities from being wrongly criminalized.

title: Insertion of Section 7-E through Finance Act, 2002
explainer:
This case concerns Section 7E of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, a provision inserted through the Finance Act, 2022, which imposed a tax on deemed income from immovable property, calculated as 5% of the fair market value of certain assets. Several petitioners challenged this provision before the Islamabad High Court, arguing it was unconstitutional.

The petitioners argued that although the law was framed as an income tax, it was in substance a tax on immovable property, something only provincial legislatures could impose after the Eighteenth Constitutional Amendment, making it beyond Parliament's power. They also argued the tax was discriminatory and confiscatory, violating constitutional rights such as the right to acquire and hold property.

The Court held that Parliament did have the constitutional authority to enact the provision, since it taxed deemed income rather than the property itself, so it was not beyond legislative competence. However, the Court found serious problems with how the law was designed: it failed to classify different types of capital assets, provided no clear method for determining fair market value, and lacked a proper mechanism for calculating or recovering the tax. This lack of clarity created arbitrary and unequal treatment among taxpayers. Because of these defects, the Court declared the provision unconstitutional and struck it down.

The case matters because it clarifies limits on how taxes must be structured to be fair, non-discriminatory, and administratively workable, even when the legislature has the power to impose them.

title: Pre-Arrest Bail in Emigration Ordinance Case
explainer:
This case involved two men, Amanat Ali and Shahid Imran, accused of fraud under the Emigration Ordinance 1979. The complainant alleged he paid them Rs. 380,000 to arrange a job for him in Malaysia in 2016. He was sent to Malaysia but no job materialized, and he had to return. An FIR was registered against the petitioners under Section 22 of the Emigration Ordinance.

Amanat Ali sought pre-arrest bail (protection from arrest), while his son Shahid Imran, who was already in custody since April 2018, sought post-arrest bail. The Lahore High Court decided both petitions together.

The court noted that no recovery of money or goods had been made directly from the petitioners during investigation, and that the money was allegedly deposited into a third party's account. It also observed that the maximum punishment under the law was 14 years imprisonment or a fine or both, meaning conviction might only result in a fine—making continued detention potentially unjust. Since investigation was complete and there was no strong evidence directly linking the petitioners to the crime, the court found the case fit for further inquiry.

The court granted post-arrest bail to Shahid Imran and confirmed pre-arrest bail for Amanat Ali, subject to bail bonds of Rs. 200,000 each with sureties. This case illustrates how courts assess sufficiency of evidence and potential punishment when deciding bail in fraud-related emigration cases.

title: Further Inquiry in case of 17(1)(2) and 22(b) Emigration Ordinance 1979
explainer:
This case is about a bail application filed by Fahad Parekh, who was accused in an FIR involving fake visa documents under the Emigration Ordinance, 1979, and sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with cheating, forgery, and abetment. The allegation was that a victim's travel documents, including his visa, were found fake, and it was revealed that the applicant and a co-accused had arranged the visa after receiving Rs. 200,000 from the victim's brother.

The applicant sought post-arrest bail, arguing that the relevant legal provisions allowed for alternate, lesser punishments, and that his co-accused had already been convicted and only fined Rs. 12,000 rather than imprisoned. The Sindh High Court agreed that since a lesser punishment was possible for these offences, the case fell outside the category of offences where bail is normally barred (the prohibitory clause), and that this matter deserved further inquiry at trial. On this basis, the court granted the applicant post-arrest bail.

The judgment also discusses broader principles about sentencing, noting that some punishments are "obligatory" and must be imposed by courts once guilt is established, while others are "discretionary." The court found that the trial court's earlier sentencing of the co-accused may have been legally flawed since mandatory imprisonment was not imposed for one of the offences. This case matters because it clarifies how courts should assess punishment severity when deciding bail, and stresses the importance of correctly applying sentencing rules.

title: Application for Impleadment in Appeal

She submitted documents including school certificates, a marriage certificate, and a divorce deed to support her claim. The Appellate Court allowed her to be included as a party and sent the whole matter back to the trial court, instructing it to properly examine her claim, take her written statement, frame issues, and record evidence before deciding the case.

Shahnaz Parveen challenged this decision, arguing that the documents relied upon were fake and forged, and that the Appellate Court should have decided the matter itself rather than sending it back.

Sending the case back to the trial court for proper examination was therefore appropriate, not a final decision affecting anyone's rights, so no grounds existed for the High Court to interfere

The Ombudsman relaxed these conditions and recommended their appointments, then directed PESCO to implement the recommendations. title: Invoking of Writ Jurisdiction in matters of Wafaqi Mohtasib
explainer:
The Habib Bank case arose from a customer complaint that a large sum of money had been fraudulently withdrawn from an account at the bank's SITE branch using forged cheques and a forged requisition slip. The customer, Pakistan Industrial Promoters, complained to the Wafaqi Mohtasib (Federal Ombudsman), alleging the bank's negligence and lack of vigilance amounted to maladministration, and asked that the fraudulent debit entries and related interest charges be reversed.

The Mohtasib agreed, finding that forgery had clearly occurred and ordering the bank to reverse the entries and interest. The bank challenged this before the President under the Ombudsman law, but that representation was rejected. The bank then approached the Sindh High Court under its constitutional writ jurisdiction, seeking to have both orders struck down.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that when action is taken under a special law like the Ombudsman Order, its validity must be judged strictly within that law's own framework and conditions. Since the Mohtasib's decision was made within the powers and procedures set out in the Ombudsman Order, the High Court found it had no jurisdiction to interfere through a writ petition.

This case matters because it clarifies the limited scope of High Court intervention in Ombudsman decisions, reinforcing that specialized statutory bodies acting within their defined powers are largely insulated from ordinary writ review.

title: Uturn of a Witness through Cross Examination
explainer:
This case comes from the Lahore High Court and involves an appeal by the State (prosecution) in a narcotics case being tried before a Special Court for Control of Narcotic Substances.

During the trial, a prosecution witness, an Inspector, gave his examination-in-chief in 2015, naming two specific individuals as the officials who had attested a recovery memo. Nearly a year later, the prosecution tried to get the witness's statement corrected, claiming an error in the names. That correction was initially allowed, but the accused challenged it, and the High Court set the correction aside, ruling the change was not a simple typo and would unfairly harm the accused. The Court noted that cross-examination on this witness had not yet taken place, and the prosecution could apply for re-examination instead.

The prosecution then applied for re-examination of the same witness, but the trial court rejected this request. The State appealed that rejection.

The High Court dismissed the appeal, holding that re-examination could not be used to let the witness reverse his earlier sworn testimony before cross-examination had even occurred. Under the law governing evidence, examination-in-chief must be followed by cross-examination, and only afterward can re-examination happen, strictly to clarify points raised in cross-examination, not to change what was already stated. Allowing otherwise would undermine the reliability of sworn testimony and open the door to manipulation of witness statements. The appeal was dismissed.

title: Review of Order of Board
explainer:
This case involved a decades-long dispute over 15 ghuntas of land in Sindh, originally leased to a man named Abdul Aziz Khan for a petrol pump, which he then rented to an oil company. Later, Abdul Aziz Khan allegedly sold the same plot to two different people at different times, leading to competing ownership claims recorded in government revenue records. When authorities investigated, a local revenue officer (EDO Revenue) found both claimed sale entries to be false and declared the land government property. On appeal, the Member Board of Revenue ruled in favor of one claimant, Abid Ali Baig, restoring his entry and rejecting the other party's claim. The losing party then filed review applications, and a different official reversed the earlier decision.

The Sindh High Court examined whether that review was legally proper. It held that the power to review a decision is very limited under the law and can only be used if new and important evidence is discovered that could not have been found earlier, or if there is an obvious mistake on the face of the record. A review cannot be used simply because someone disagrees with how the law was applied or facts were assessed, since that would turn review into an endless appeal process. Finding no such new evidence or apparent error, the court ruled the review was not valid and restored the original order in favor of Abid Ali Baig.

This case matters because it clarifies that review powers are narrow and cannot be misused as a backdoor appeal, ensuring finality and fairness in administrative and revenue decisions.

title: Re-Examination is more important than examination
explainer:
This Lahore High Court decision deals with a criminal case in which the accused, Mehdi Khan, was on trial for murder along with other offences. The complainant, while testifying as a prosecution witness in a retrial of the case, said he could not remember details he had earlier given about calling the police to the scene, which he had stated clearly in his cross-examination during an earlier trial. The defence wanted to confront him with that earlier statement, but the trial court refused, reasoning that since the witness had not mentioned this detail in his fresh examination-in-chief, it could not be treated as an improvement warranting confrontation, and that facts brought out only in cross-examination could not be used this way.

The High Court disagreed and set aside the trial court's order. It held that examination of a witness legally includes examination-in-chief, cross-examination, and re-examination, and that cross-examination is in fact more important than examination-in-chief because it tests credibility and can reveal facts the witness concealed or omitted. Since the complainant claimed not to remember his earlier statement, the defence had every right to confront him with what he had said before. Relying on a Supreme Court precedent, the court ruled that denying this right was legally unsound.

The judgment matters because it reinforces the right of the defence to fully test a witness's credibility through cross-examination and confrontation with prior statements, a key safeguard in ensuring fair trials.

title: Re-Examination is more important than Examination in Chief
explainer:
This is a Sindh High Court judgment deciding a criminal jail appeal by Abdul Latif, who was convicted alongside a co-accused for murder under Section 302/34 of the Pakistan Penal Code. The complainant alleged that his brother was shot during a scuffle involving armed men, and the accused were later arrested nearby.

The appellant's lawyer raised two main objections. First, that the framed charge was defective because it did not properly detail how Sections 222 and 223 of the Criminal Procedure Code required it to be framed. Second, and more significantly, that a key prosecution witness was examined in court but never properly cross-examined, since he was absent on the date the trial judge wrongly recorded that defense counsel was "not ready" to cross-examine him.

The court rejected the defective-charge argument, finding the charge gave the accused sufficient notice of the case against him, and noted this objection was never raised during trial. However, the court took the missed cross-examination very seriously. It held that cross-examination is not merely a formality but arguably more important than the initial examination of a witness, since it tests the truthfulness and credibility of testimony, especially crucial in capital punishment cases. The court ruled that speedy trials must not compromise fairness, and judges must ensure genuine testing of evidence rather than assuming rights were satisfied. The case was sent back to the trial court so the witness could finally be properly cross-examined.

title: Favouritism in Qualification for bids cannot be allowed
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the privatisation of SME Bank Ltd, a government-owned bank. The Privatisation Commission had invited investors to submit Expressions of Interest and then Statements of Qualification, with a deadline that was extended once, from March 17 to April 7, 2017, after several early applicants requested more time. The petitioners, Saifco Group, only came forward on April 6, 2017, one day before the extended deadline, and applied for the qualification documents. They received these documents on April 7 but were told to submit their qualification statement that same day. They asked for a further extension until April 17, which the Commission refused, leading them to challenge that refusal in the Islamabad High Court.

The court dismissed the petition. It held that further extending the deadline solely to accommodate the petitioners, who had applied very late compared to other bidders, would amount to unfair favouritism and would violate procurement rules requiring transparency and equal treatment of all bidders. The judge said courts cannot rewrite the terms of a public tender to suit a party's convenience, and that the petitioners' own delay was responsible for their predicament, invoking the principle that "delay defeats equity."

The case matters because it reinforces that public bidding processes must remain fair and consistent for all participants, and courts will not intervene to grant special treatment to latecomers at the expense of other competitors.

title: PPSC is required to fill vacant posts in a transparent manner through competitive examination
explainer:
This case involved candidates applying for the post of Assistant District Public Prosecutor (ADPP) through the Punjab Public Service Commission (PPSC). The advertisement set an age limit of 25 to 35 years, but used 1 January 2017 as the cut-off date for calculating age eligibility, while using a later date, 14 September 2017, for calculating experience eligibility. The petitioners argued this was unfair because they were technically underage on 1 January 2017 but became eligible before the later date. They also pointed out that previous advertisements for the same post in 2011, 2012, 2015 and 2016 never used any age cut-off date at all, so the sudden change felt arbitrary and discriminatory.

The Lahore High Court examined the relevant rule, which actually required age to be calculated as of 1 January of the exam year for written competitive tests. This rule existed since 1976, but PPSC had simply failed to follow it for years until it introduced a formal policy decision in October 2016. The court held that PPSC, as a statutory body, must recruit transparently through competitive examination and follow its own rules. However, because PPSC had been inconsistent for years and failed to properly publicize the changed policy, it would be unfair to penalize applicants who relied on the old practice. The court ruled that anyone who was underage on 1 January 2017 or became overage after that date could still compete, as long as they met the age requirement by the actual application deadline of 14 September 2017. It also directed PPSC to properly publicize its policies going forward through its website and newspapers.

title: Contract which is in its nature revocable cannot be specifically enforced
explainer:
This case comes from the Sindh High Court and involves a business dispute over tractor imports. The plaintiffs, a trading company and a joint venture firm, claimed they had partnered with certain defendants to import Belarus-made tractors into Pakistan and set up an assembly plant, based on a memorandum of understanding and joint venture agreement signed in January 2015. They alleged that some of the defendants secretly formed a rival company for the same business purpose, cutting them out and breaching their agreement. The plaintiffs asked the court to grant an injunction stopping the defendants from dealing with the tractor manufacturer or carrying on the tractor business except through them.

The court refused to grant the injunction. It held that specific performance of a contract cannot be ordered where the contract is, by its nature, revocable, and that specific performance is a discretionary equitable remedy, not something granted automatically. The judge found the plaintiffs had not shown a strong prima facie case, since they had not even attached the company's articles of association to support their claims, and a related complaint was already pending before the securities regulator, which could take its own action if wrongdoing was found. The court also noted that where a dispute is essentially about money and compensation could adequately address any loss, no injunction should be issued, since injunctions require proof of a prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable harm - none of which were sufficiently established here.

title: PLJ 2018 Quetta 82 (DB)
explainer:
This case involved a custody dispute over two children following the dissolution of their parents' marriage. The mother had originally filed for divorce, dowry recovery, and maintenance, and the family court granted her a khula divorce along with monthly maintenance for the children, though it rejected her dowry claim. That decision was upheld on appeal.

Later, the mother filed a separate application asking the court to order the father to take custody of the two children, Ahmedullah (about 13) and Bibi Mariam (about 8). She explained that she had entered into a new nikah with another man and, though the marriage was not yet fully consummated (rukhsati pending), she felt the father should take the children, citing her poor financial circumstances compared to the father's better means. The trial court dismissed her application, and she challenged that dismissal before the High Court.

The High Court explained the Islamic law principle that a mother normally has the right of custody (hizanat) of her children, but this right ends if she remarries a man who is a stranger to the children, unless the child's welfare requires otherwise. Since the mother had remarried, she lost her custody right specifically over the daughter, Bibi Mariam. However, since the son, Ahmedullah, was already about 13 years old, the age-based custody rules relevant to hizanat did not affect him. The court accepted the petition on this basis.

This case matters because it clarifies how remarriage affects a mother's custody rights under Muslim family law, while emphasizing that the child's welfare remains the guiding consideration.

title: PLJ 2017 Quetta 58 (DB)
explainer:
This case involved a husband who challenged a legal provision after his wife filed for divorce through khula (a wife's right to seek dissolution of marriage) in a family court in Islamabad.

The husband, Naeem Sher Tareen, approached the Balochistan High Court asking it to declare Section 10(4) of the Family Courts Act 1964 illegal and un-Islamic, to stop family courts from applying it, to direct the government to make laws in line with Sharia, and to limit divorce cases to only the grounds listed in the Dissolution of Marriage Act 1939. He also wanted his wife's pending family case transferred from Islamabad to Quetta. In pursuing this, he had named the President of Pakistan, the National Assembly, and the Senate as respondents.

The High Court dismissed the petition on two main grounds. First, under Article 203-G of the Constitution, courts like the High Court have no jurisdiction to decide whether a law is repugnant to Islamic injunctions - that power belongs exclusively to the Federal Shariat Court under Article 203-D. Second, the request to transfer the case from Islamabad to Quetta could not be granted because the Islamabad family court falls outside the territorial jurisdiction of the Balochistan High Court.

This case matters because it clarifies that constitutional courts cannot rule on whether legislation conforms to Islamic law, and that courts cannot order transfers of cases from jurisdictions outside their own territorial authority.

title: Entitlement of Father to Custody of Male Child
explainer:
This case involved a custody dispute over an eight-year-old boy named Rehan, whose parents Tahira Zaib and Ghaffar Ahmed had divorced. Both parents had since remarried. The father applied for custody of the child, while the mother sought to cancel his guardianship certificate and have herself appointed guardian instead. The Guardian Judge at Kotli ruled in favor of the father, and the mother appealed to the Azad Jammu and Kashmir High Court.

The mother argued the child had lived with her since birth and barely knew his father, and that under Islamic law a mother is entitled to custody of a male child until he turns seven. The father countered that both he and the child were British nationals, and that it would benefit the child's education and upbringing to live with him in the UK.

The High Court dismissed the mother's appeal and upheld the father's guardianship. It reasoned that the welfare of the child is the most important consideration in custody cases, that the mother had no shown means to financially support the child, and that the UK, being a welfare state, would help ensure the child's wellbeing even if the father struggled to pay maintenance. The court also noted the boy was of school-going age and would benefit from better educational opportunities in the UK, concluding that his welfare lay with his father.

title: PLJ 2015 Lahore 1201
explainer:
This case involved a woman, Kausar Parveen, whose husband filed a criminal complaint (FIR) against her and the man she later married, Samar Khan, accusing them of offenses including adultery, theft, and unlawful marriage. The husband claimed she was still legally his wife when she married someone else.

The facts showed Kausar Parveen had gone through two rounds of legal proceedings to dissolve her marriage. Her second suit for dissolution was decided in her favor by a Family Court on 6 September 2013, and she remarried the very next day. The husband tried to argue that she had later withdrawn her consent to that divorce, but the court found the documents supporting this claim were undated, unclear, and never followed by any formal court order, so they were disregarded.

The key legal question was whether her second marriage was valid, void, or merely irregular, given it happened so soon after the divorce. The court explained that under Islamic law, marrying before completing the mandatory waiting period (iddat) makes a marriage irregular, not void — and iddat is only required if the earlier marriage had been physically consummated or ended by death. Since the couple had already been separated for months before her remarriage, no criminality existed.

The Lahore High Court ruled that the FIR was based on wrong premises, with no real evidence of a crime, and quashed it entirely, stopping all further legal proceedings against the couple. This case reaffirms that a technical delay in waiting periods does not automatically criminalize a lawful marriage.

title: PLJ 2015 Karachi 241 (DB)
explainer:
This case involved a bitter custody dispute between divorced parents over their young daughter. The mother had custody of the child since birth, and family courts (trial court, appellate court, and even the High Court in an earlier petition) had all confirmed her right to custody, known in Islamic law as hizanat. While a custody case was still pending, the mother took the child to the USA to pursue admission in an American university for postgraduate studies, as her career prospects depended on it. The father, upset that his access to the child was being denied, filed a police case (FIR) accusing the mother and her relatives of kidnapping his daughter, and separately sought Interpol assistance to have them arrested and extradited.

The mother and her family asked the High Court to cancel the FIR, arguing that a mother cannot be prosecuted for kidnapping her own child when she already lawfully has custody.

The High Court agreed and quashed the FIR. It held that both parents are natural guardians of their child, and one natural guardian cannot accuse the other of kidnapping when there was no snatching of custody involved. The court clarified that a father's guardianship doesn't disappear just because the mother has custody, and he retains rights of access and financial responsibility, while the mother's custody rights don't disappear either. The court emphasized that criminal kidnapping charges are not the appropriate tool to resolve custody disputes between parents, which should instead be handled through family courts. This ruling protects parents with lawful custody from being criminally prosecuted by the other parent during custody disagreements.

title: PLJ 2015 FSC 33
explainer:
This case was heard by the Federal Shariat Court, where a petitioner challenged Section 5 of the West Pakistan Family Courts Act, 1964. This section gives Family Courts the power to hear and decide various marital matters, including cases about restitution of conjugal rights, meaning orders that a wife should return to live with her husband. The petitioner's lawyer argued that this power was against Islamic teachings, saying courts should not be able to force an unwilling wife to live with her husband, and instead should focus on reconciliation between spouses.

The court examined this argument alongside a verse from the Quran (Surah Al-Nisa, Verse 35) about appointing arbitrators to reconcile estranged spouses. The judges agreed that reconciliation is encouraged by Islamic teachings and noted that the law itself already provides for compromise attempts before and during trial. However, they found that when reconciliation fails, the law appropriately allows courts to resolve the dispute through other means, including restitution of conjugal rights orders.

The court asked the lawyer to point to a specific Quranic verse or Hadith that prohibited such orders, but he could not do so. The judges reasoned that leaving marital disputes unresolved indefinitely would cause hardship, especially regarding maintenance and child custody. They suggested that if reconciliation truly fails, divorce or khula (wife-initiated divorce) is the proper solution rather than removing the court's power entirely.

The petition was dismissed, meaning the law was upheld as consistent with Islamic inj

title: Commission of Offense outside Pakistan
explainer:
This case involved a challenge to the registration of a criminal case (FIR) against a company under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with dishonoured cheques issued with dishonest intent. The petitioner argued that since the alleged offence occurred outside Pakistan (in the UAE, where a civil court had already decided a related dispute), the case could not be registered without proper sanction under Section 188 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which governs offences committed outside Pakistan. He also argued that the cheques were issued company-to-company, not individual-to-individual, and questioned the validity of Section 489-F itself.

The Lahore High Court rejected these arguments. It held that Section 188 procedures were not strictly required here, since no political agent existed in the UAE and any needed government sanction could still be obtained even after formal charges were filed. The court also ruled that registering an FIR does not depend on whether the underlying facts are ultimately true or false, only on whether the complaint discloses a cognizable offence, a matter to be settled through investigation, not through court intervention at this stage.

Importantly, the court criticized the Sessions Judge for making premature findings suggesting guilt, and directed the investigating officer to ignore those remarks and conduct a fair, independent investigation per Police Rules. The petition was dismissed, reinforcing that courts should not interfere with or influence police investigations before they are complete.

title: PLJ 2018 SC 180
explainer:
This case involved the tragic killing of a young man, Shahzeb Khan, who was shot dead after coming to defend his sister from harassment by a servant of an influential accused family. After the accused's conviction, the case became controversial when the accused left the country without joining the investigation, sparking public protests and heavy media coverage. Initially tried and decided in an Anti-Terrorism Court, the case was later sent by the Sindh High Court back to an ordinary court for a fresh trial, on the reasoning that the killing stemmed from personal enmity rather than terrorism.

Members of civil society challenged this before the Supreme Court, which converted their appeals into a suo motu case under Article 184(3) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that motive or personal enmity is not the deciding factor for whether the Anti-Terrorism Act applies; what matters is whether the act created fear, panic, and insecurity among the public. Since the killing caused widespread fear and public unrest, the case rightly fell under the Anti-Terrorism Court's jurisdiction.

The Court set aside the High Court's order sending the case for retrial in an ordinary court, revived the original proceedings before the High Court, and ordered previously bailed convicts to be taken back into custody, since their release had no legal basis. This judgment clarifies that public impact, not personal motive, determines whether a crime qualifies as terrorism under Pakistani law.

title: PLJ 2018 Islamabad 143
explainer:
This case involved a dispute among siblings over their late mother's property. After Razia Sultana died in 2005, her son Sohail Ahmed Jan sued his brothers and sisters, claiming he was entitled to inherit a share in several properties, including two houses in Islamabad and Rawalpindi and some savings certificates. He argued that his mother had never validly transferred these properties during her lifetime, and that the transfer documents showing gifts to his sister and brother were fraudulent and manipulated.

The trial court dismissed his suit, and an appellate court partly modified that decision but still ruled against him. He then approached the Islamabad High Court.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It found that his allegations of fraud were vague and lacked the specific details required by law when fraud is alleged. It also explained that under Islamic law, a valid gift only requires three things: a declaration by the giver, acceptance by the receiver, and delivery of possession—no written deed is legally necessary, and a parent can gift property even while continuing to live in it, as constructive possession suffices. The court found that the transfer of the properties to the respondents met these requirements and was properly recorded as a "family transfer" under CDA regulations.

This judgment matters because it clarifies how courts assess claims of fraud in property disputes and reaffirms the flexible, non-technical requirements for valid gifts under Islamic law, especially within families.

title: Time Spent in Litigation at wrong forum is exempted
explainer:

The Tribunal held that it had the power to exclude this time spent litigating in the wrong forum when calculating whether the appeal was filed within the limitation period. However, since the appellant still could not explain an additional two-month delay after the High Court's decision, his appeal was ultimately held to be time-barred.

Therefore workmen employed by WAPDA, like other WAPDA employees, were governed instead by WAPDA's own Efficiency and Discipline Rules, under which the appellant's termination (following his conviction and sentence by a Summary Military Court) was valid.

title: Rent Controller cannot determine title of property

Ahmad Ali claimed he owned a shop in Quetta, had rented it to Nasar-ud-din since 1983, and later found the tenant had defaulted on rent, sublet the property, and that he himself needed the shop back. The tenant denied being a tenant at all, claiming he had actually purchased the shop from Ahmad Ali after their business partnership ended.

The Rent Controller initially ruled in favor of the owner and ordered eviction. The Balochistan High Court reversed this, dismissing the eviction case. The matter then went to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court sided with the owner, restoring the eviction order. It clarified an important legal principle: while a Rent Controller cannot act like a civil court and formally decide disputed questions of property title, the Rent Controller can still determine whether a landlord-tenant relationship exists between the parties. If a person claiming to be an owner (rather than a tenant) fails to produce solid documentary proof of that ownership claim, the Rent Controller can proceed on the basis that the landlord-tenant relationship exists.

In this case, the tenant could not prove he had purchased the shop, while the owner had official allotment and payment records from the Quetta Development Authority. The Court held that in the absence of contrary evidence, the person with title is presumed to be the landlord, and the occupant is presumed to be the tenant. title: Heroin Case Judgment PLJ 1997 FSC 64
explainer:
This case involved a woman named Mst. Nargis who was convicted of drug trafficking under Pakistan's Prohibition (Enforcement of Hadd) Order, 1979. Police claimed that in August 1994, they stopped a passenger coach and a female constable found a packet containing 500 grams of heroin in the appellant's possession. A small sample was sent for chemical testing, which confirmed it was heroin, while the bulk of the seized substance was destroyed on a magistrate's orders. A trial court convicted her, sentencing her to five years' imprisonment, ten stripes, and a fine.

On appeal, her lawyer argued that the actual seized drugs, the physical case property, were never produced in court during the trial. Even the 15 grams that had been kept aside after the rest was destroyed were never shown as evidence. The Federal Shariat Court agreed this was a serious problem. It held that the State has a duty to produce all necessary evidence to prove guilt beyond doubt, and since no physical drug evidence was ever presented in court, the case had become doubtful.

Because the benefit of doubt must go to the accused, the court accepted the appeal, set aside her conviction and sentence, and ordered her acquittal and release. This case matters because it reinforces an important legal principle: prosecutors cannot secure a conviction, especially for serious drug offenses, without actually presenting the physical evidence in court, no matter what other testimony or paperwork exists.

title: Grandparents are not responsible for maintenance in presence of father
explainer:
This case involved a father who challenged a court order requiring him to pay maintenance for his three minor children, including maintenance for a past period going back to 1982.

A family court initially dismissed the mother's claim for maintenance, but an appellate court reversed this and awarded maintenance to the children from the date the case was filed. When the matter reached the High Court through a constitutional petition, the court went further and granted maintenance covering the full period from 1982. The father appealed this decision to the Supreme Court on two grounds: first, that past maintenance (for a period before the court case was filed) could not legally be awarded to children, and second, that since the children were being supported by their grandparents, he should not have to pay.

The Supreme Court rejected both arguments. On the first point, it held that if wives can be awarded past maintenance, there is no legal reason to deny the same benefit to children, as excluding them would be unfair. On the second point, the court ruled that grandparents only become responsible for supporting grandchildren when no closer, more responsible relative exists. Since the father was alive and available, he remained primarily responsible for his children's upkeep, regardless of any support the grandparents were providing.

The appeal was dismissed, confirming that fathers cannot avoid their maintenance obligations by pointing to other relatives who happen to be helping out, and that children, like wives, can claim maintenance for past periods.

title: Six Days Delay in Lodging FIR
explainer:
This case involved a bail-before-arrest application before the Lahore High Court, filed by two petitioners accused of abduction under Section 365 of the Pakistan Penal Code.

The background: a woman's son had married the daughter of one petitioner against her family's wishes. Shortly after, the petitioners themselves filed a criminal case against the complainant's side, alleging abduction and, later, rape. The complainant then filed this FIR against the petitioners, but only six days after the alleged incident, a delay that was never explained.

The court found several reasons to doubt the case against the petitioners. The unexplained six-day delay in filing the FIR raised suspicion. The timing suggested the complainant's FIR may have been filed to counter the case the petitioners had already lodged against her side. Although the alleged victim claimed she was beaten after being abducted, there was no medical certificate (MLC) supporting this claim. The judge noted that false implication of the petitioners, possibly with police involvement, could not be ruled out. Additionally, the petitioners had no prior criminal record.

Based on these factors, the court confirmed the pre-arrest bail already granted earlier, requiring bail bonds of Rs. 50,000 each with sureties.

This case matters because it illustrates how courts scrutinize delays in FIR registration and weigh competing criminal complaints between feuding parties, especially in disputes arising from marriages opposed by families, to prevent misuse of the criminal justice system for retaliation.

title: General Principle is Bail not Jail
explainer:
This case is about whether a man accused of injuring a woman during a family dispute should be granted bail while awaiting trial. Abdul Razzaq was accused, along with several relatives, of attacking a complainant's mother, allegedly fracturing her arm with a stone during a quarrel that started over an accusation of grass-cutting on someone's land. He was charged with several offences, including causing a specific type of injury under the Pakistan Penal Code.

The trial court and a district court had refused him bail, and the Shariat Court (a lower appellate court) upheld that refusal, mistakenly citing a legal provision that carried a 10-year maximum sentence, which would have placed the case in a category where bail is harder to get. However, the actual charge against Razzaq carried a maximum punishment of only 7 years, meaning his case did not fall into that stricter category.

The Supreme Court of Azad Jammu and Kashmir found that the lower court had made an error in identifying which law applied. Since the correct charge did not carry a 10-year sentence, the general legal principle applies: bail should be granted, not refused, unless there are extraordinary reasons to keep someone in custody. The court also noted inconsistencies in the prosecution's case, including an unexplained 23-hour delay in filing the police report despite witnesses being present. Since Razzaq had already been detained for over five months without any witnesses being examined by the trial court, he was granted bail.

During his trial, when his lawyer failed to appear in court to cross-examine prosecution witnesses, the trial court simply closed his right to cross-examine those witnesses altogether. In some instances, the court even asked the accused himself to conduct the cross-examination rather than a qualified lawyer.

Hussain challenged this decision before the Lahore High Court, arguing that even if his lawyer was unavailable, the court should have arranged a state-funded lawyer to represent him, especially given the seriousness of the charges.

The High Court agreed with him. It ruled that while speedy trials are desirable, rushing justice at the cost of fairness is unacceptable, famously noting that justice hurried is justice buried. The court held that when an accused's lawyer doesn't show up, the trial court should either adjourn the hearing briefly or appoint a lawyer at state expense, rather than penalizing the accused. It also strongly criticized the practice of asking an accused person to personally cross-examine witnesses, stating this can never substitute for cross-examination by a trained lawyer.

The court set aside the trial court's order and directed that Hussain be given a proper opportunity to arrange legal representation for cross-examining witnesses. title: Eviction of Tenant in case notice is not served under section 19
citation: PLD 1964 SC 536; Major (Recd.) Muhammad Yousuf v. Mehraj-ud-Din and
explainer:
Sher Jang was a tenant occupying shops and a residential flat in Islamabad. The original owner, Najeebullah Khan, had transferred the property to his sons, who then filed a case to evict the tenant for not paying rent from June 2001 onward. The tenant argued he should not be evicted because the new owners never sent him the formal notice about the change of ownership required under section 19 of the Islamabad Rent Restriction Ordinance, 2000. He claimed he had been paying rent to the original owner and only agreed to recognize the sons as landlords going forward.

The Rent Controller and the District Judge both ruled against the tenant, and the High Court upheld the eviction. The case reached the Supreme Court, which had to decide whether a tenant can be evicted for non-payment of rent even without proper notice under section 19, and whether earlier Supreme Court rulings on this issue conflicted with each other.

The Supreme Court held that even without a separate notice, the ejectment petition itself could count as sufficient notice under section 19. It also found that the tenant behaved badly by refusing to pay rent as directed by the Court and by disputing the landlord-tenant relationship, so he wasn't entitled to any special leniency. The Court refused to grant further appeal, meaning the eviction order stood. This case clarifies how rent notice rules apply when property ownership changes hands and stresses that tenants must comply with court orders to get relief.

title: Inheritance of illegitimate child
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over inheritance rights within a Pakistani family. After a man died, his brother (the children's uncle) challenged the legitimacy of the deceased's children, claiming they were not really his brother's offspring and therefore had no right to inherit his property. The uncle had gone along with the children being recognized as heirs when the inheritance mutation was first recorded, raising no objection at that time. Only later, apparently to grab a piece of land, did he begin disputing their parentage, and he even said he would accept them as legitimate if they gave up their inheritance claim.

The court rejected the uncle's case. It found no evidence that the children's mother had been divorced before their birth or was living in adultery. Under Islamic law (Sunni jurisprudence), a child born within six months of marriage's start, or within two years of its dissolution, is legally presumed legitimate. The uncle also never used the proper legal procedure (called Liyan, swearing before a judge) to formally accuse the mother of adultery and disown the children. Since the father himself never denied paternity during his lifetime, the court held the children were legitimate and fully entitled to inherit their father's estate.

The case matters because it reinforces protections for children's inheritance rights

title: Bail Confirmed on 45 days delay in Lodging FIR
explainer:
This case involves Muhammad Rafique, who was accused of stealing four cattle from a complainant's shed in Multan. An FIR was registered against him and another person under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with theft and dishonestly receiving stolen property. However, the FIR was filed one and a half months after the cattle went missing, and this delay was never explained by the complainant.

The Lahore High Court found several problems with the prosecution's case. There was no explanation of how the complainant suddenly came to know that the petitioner was involved in the theft. Additionally, the investigating officer admitted that the stolen cattle had actually been recovered earlier under a separate legal provision, having been left behind by unidentified persons, well before the FIR was even filed. This raised doubts about whether the story linking the petitioner to the crime was genuine.

The court also noted that the investigating officer confirmed nothing remained to be recovered from the petitioner, that the investigation was already complete, and that the case had been sent to trial but had not yet begun. The petitioner had no prior criminal record, and the charges did not fall under the more serious category of offenses that would normally block bail.

Given these doubts and the lack of prior convictions, the court ruled that the matter required further inquiry at trial and confirmed the petitioner's pre-arrest bail, requiring him to post a bond of Rs. 50,000 with a surety.

title: Jurisdiction of High Court in cases of Promotion of Civil Servants
explainer:
This case concerns a civil servant, Nawabzada Muhammad Nadir Khan Hoti, who was passed over for promotion to a senior grade (BPS-21) by the Central Selection Board (CSB). The Board's reasons included allegations that he was involved in improper sales tax refunds and did not enjoy a good reputation. However, the petitioner showed that these very allegations had earlier been withdrawn by the tax department itself, and an inquiry against him had been vacated, meaning no charges were actually pending against him when the CSB made its decision.

The government argued that the Peshawar High Court had no jurisdiction to hear the case, since civil servants' service matters are normally handled by the Federal Service Tribunal, and since the decision was made in Islamabad, not within the court's territorial area. The court rejected both objections. It held that questions about a civil servant's "fitness" for promotion are excluded from the Service Tribunal's jurisdiction and can be examined by the High Court, and that territorial jurisdiction under Article 199 is not limited by ordinary civil procedure rules when federal bodies operate nationwide.

On the merits, the court found that the CSB acted unfairly by relying on discredited allegations without giving the petitioner evidence or a chance to respond, violating the fundamental right to fair and transparent procedure under Article 10-A. The court ruled in his favor, following a similar precedent from the same CSB meeting, reinforcing that promotion decisions must be based on solid, verified evidence and fair procedure.

title: Powers of Court in Execution Proceedings
explainer:

When Farooq failed to pay the full decretal amount, he was sent to civil prison but released after paying part of it and providing a surety (Mehboob Ahmed) for the rest. Later, Qamar-uz-Zaman returned from abroad, cancelled the power of attorney, and claimed he was not responsible. Both the attorney and the surety also tried to get released from liability, but the Executing Court and the Additional District Judge rejected their applications, holding them responsible for the balance. They then challenged this in the Lahore High Court.

It held that decrees, especially from Family Courts, must be enforced effectively, using recovery procedures similar to those for land revenue arrears, and that debtors cannot use technicalities to escape execution.

title: Latest Judgment in a Defamation Case
citation: PLD 1981 Kar. 515; Mazhar Valjee v. Sher Afghan Khan Niazi 2004 YLR
explainer:
This case involved a defamation lawsuit brought by the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan against a newspaper, Khabrain, and its publishers (Liberty Papers Ltd). The newspaper had published a story on 8 March 2004 falsely and maliciously claiming that office bearers of the Human Rights Commission were instigating violence, spreading anti-military sentiments through financial rewards, and that certain groups were subsidiaries of the organization. The trial court awarded the Commission five million rupees in damages, and on appeal the Balochistan High Court reduced this to one million rupees. The newspaper then appealed to the Supreme Court of Pakistan.

The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, dismissing the newspaper's appeal. It held that the allegations were serious because they accused public figures of conspiring against the state through underhanded means, and that the newspaper had nationwide circulation, causing significant reputational and financial harm. The Court also clarified important legal principles: plaintiffs in defamation cases can sue wherever the material was published or significantly circulated; newspapers must prove they acted diligently and followed ethical journalistic standards to claim a "good faith" defense; and failure to prove the truth of published claims can itself indicate malice, justifying aggravated damages. The judgment emphasizes that protecting personal dignity is a constitutional obligation, and media freedom does not excuse irresponsible or unverified reporting.

title: Zina Case Judgment
explainer:

The background: Kalsoom Mai had earlier filed a petition alleging that Ashiq and others committed zina-bil-jabr against her. Police investigated and found her allegations false, and she later withdrew the petition, with reports suggesting the parties had reached a compromise. Ashiq then filed his own complaint accusing her and others of qazf, arguing they had falsely accused him. A trial court judge dismissed his complaint at the outset, noting he waited 21 months to file it and that legal requirements for a qazf case were not met.

On appeal, the Federal Shariat Court upheld the dismissal. It found that Kalsoom Mai never appeared in court or gave any statement, so there was no formal finding by any court that she had lied or made a false accusation, which is required under the law. The mere fact her original complaint included her photograph did not prove she authored it. The court also noted Ashiq and his co-accused had been acquitted in the related criminal case due to doubts in the prosecution's evidence, not because anyone was proven to have lied.

title: Quashing of FIR Judgment
explainer:
This case is about a petition asking the Sindh High Court to cancel a First Information Report (FIR) registered against Wajid Ali Memon and others under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with rioting, criminal force, wrongful restraint, criminal intimidation, and also under the Anti-Terrorism Act.

The FIR arose from an incident where a Magistrate, acting on court orders to search for a missing person, was blocked by a crowd at a house, faced threats, and had someone attempt to snatch his guard's weapon. Based on this report, a Single Judge had earlier directed police to register an FIR, including charges under the Anti-Terrorism Act.

The Division Bench of the High Court, hearing the petition to quash the FIR, examined the facts and found that the elements required for terrorism charges (Sections 6/7 of the Anti-Terrorism Act) and for criminal intimidation (Section 506(ii) PPC) were not actually present, since mere threats without the specific ingredients of criminal intimidation are not enough. The court ruled these particular sections should be deleted from the case, meaning it would be handled by a regular court instead of an anti-terrorism court.

However, the court did not quash the entire FIR. It held that quashing an FIR is only appropriate when the evidence, even if fully believed, could not support any conviction. Since the case was still pending trial, the petitioner was told to pursue his remedies before the trial court instead.

title: Perjury is not allowed in the court of law
explainer:
This Supreme Court of Pakistan judgment dealt with the case of Muhammad Aslam, who was convicted of murdering his uncle, Mehdi Hassan. The motive was revenge: years earlier, when Aslam was a small child, his father had disappeared and was suspected to have been killed by his own step-brother, the same Mehdi Hassan. When Aslam grew into his teens, he shot and killed Mehdi Hassan in public, declaring he had avenged his father's death.

The Lahore High Court had upheld his conviction and death sentence. The Supreme Court agreed he was guilty but reduced his sentence from death to life imprisonment, taking into account that he committed the act while still very young, avenging a killing that had happened when he was only two or three years old. However, the Court found the fine imposed too low and raised it from Rs. 2,000 to Rs. 25,000, to be paid as compensation to the deceased's heirs if recovered.

Separately, the Court addressed perjury. It found that two witnesses, one for the prosecution and one for the defence, had lied under oath during the trial. The judges strongly condemned false testimony, stressing that courts must punish perjury firmly to deter others, since lying in court undermines public trust in the justice system. The Supreme Court directed the trial court to initiate proceedings against both witnesses under the law dealing with false evidence.

title: Justice of Peace is not required to allow petition blindly
explainer:
This case from the Peshawar High Court dealt with a dispute over the registration of a criminal case (FIR) by police. The petitioner, Qamar Naeem, claimed he owned a shop that he had rented out to another person. He alleged that certain accused individuals, armed with weapons, forcibly broke the lock of the shop and attacked him. When he approached the police to register a case, they instead began an inquiry rather than registering an FIR. He then approached the Justice of Peace under Section 22-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, asking for a direction to register the case, but this request was rejected.

The High Court found that the facts described by the petitioner clearly disclosed a cognizable offence, meaning the police had a legal duty to register an FIR without first investigating or hearing the accused's side. The court explained that while a Justice of Peace has power to review such police inaction, this power is limited: he should not dive into disputed facts, nor should he approve or reject requests automatically without proper legal reasoning. However, if the complainant's allegations clearly show a cognizable offence, refusing to register the case is arbitrary and improper.

The court therefore quashed the Justice of Peace's order and directed the police to register the FIR. This judgment matters because it clarifies the limited role of a Justice of Peace and reinforces those with genuine complaints disclosing criminal offences cannot be denied FIR registration through overly cautious or dismissive judicial review.

title: Custody of Minor by Grandmother
explainer:
This case was about who should have custody of a young boy after his father died: his mother or his paternal grandmother. After the father's death, the mother lived with her in-laws, but the grandmother later forced her out of the house while keeping the child. The mother first sought the child's recovery through the courts, but her petition was dismissed because the boy said he preferred living with his grandmother. She then filed a separate case asking to be made his legal guardian, which was also initially dismissed on the same grounds. On appeal, though, the earlier decision was overturned, and the court ordered that custody be given to the mother. The grandmother challenged this in the High Court.

The High Court upheld the decision in the mother's favor. It found that the child appeared to have been influenced against his mother, even inventing false claims of abuse, and that the grandmother had not followed the court's visitation arrangements and seemed to be encouraging the child to lie and harbor hatred. The judge stressed that harm to a child isn't only physical but can be psychological too. It noted the mother's sacrifices, her stability, and that under Islamic law a grandmother's right to custody is secondary to the mother's. Ultimately, the court held that the child's true welfare lay with his mother, and dismissed the grandmother's petition. The case underscores that in custody disputes, the child's actual best interests—not just their stated preference—must guide the court's decision.

title: Judgment on Inheritance of Consanguine Sisters
explainer:
This case involves a dispute over inheritance following the death of Ali Haider Khan, who died without children. His widow and one full sister (the appellants) claimed they alone were entitled to his property, arguing that his other siblings, described as step-brothers and step-sisters, should be excluded as residuary heirs under Islamic inheritance law. The respondents were these step-siblings, who had also applied for a succession certificate to claim their share.

The trial court had already divided the estate: the widow received one-fourth, the full sister received one-half, and the remaining share was split among the four step-brothers and two step-sisters. The widow and sister appealed, arguing that under Mohammadan Law, specifically Section 109, uterine (half) siblings sharing only a mother with the deceased are excluded from inheriting any "return" share if a full sister exists.

The High Court dismissed the appeal. It clarified that Section 109 only excludes uterine siblings, not consanguine siblings, who share a father with the deceased. Since the respondents were consanguine, not uterine, siblings, the rule the appellants relied on did not apply to them. The court also noted that a party cannot argue a position contrary to what it originally pleaded.

This judgment matters because it clarifies an important distinction in Islamic inheritance law between uterine and consanguine siblings, confirming that consanguine siblings are not automatically excluded from inheritance shares even when a full sister survives the deceased.

title: Direct Appeal against Election Petition Allowed by Supreme Court
explainer:
This case is about a challenge to the 2008 National Assembly election result from a constituency in Khushab, Punjab. Malik Umar Aslam, who lost narrowly to Mrs. Sumaira Malik, filed an election petition alleging vote manipulation and, crucially, that Malik's BA degree - required at the time to qualify as a candidate - was fake, obtained through impersonation rather than her actually sitting the exams.

The Election Tribunal had dismissed his petition, so he appealed directly to the Supreme Court under the Representation of the People Act, 1976.

The Supreme Court examined evidence including signatures, photographs on university admission and registration forms, and attendance records, comparing them under the Qanun-e-Shahadat (evidence law). It found that the degree had indeed been secured through impersonation and fraud, meaning Malik did not actually meet the graduation requirement in place for the 2002 elections under the Conduct of General Election Order. The Court held that a candidate must satisfy the constitutional character requirements of being honest, righteous and non-profligate, and that obtaining a degree through fraud meant she failed this test and was never validly qualified to hold the seat.

As a result, the Court ruled she was not lawfully holding her seat, could not benefit from the disputed election, and would be barred from contesting future elections too - with the Election Commission required to unseat her if she were ever declared elected again. This case is significant because it reinforced strict scrutiny of candidates' educational credentials and moral qualifications for public office.

title: Concept of Suspension of Sentence
explainer:
This Lahore High Court (Multan Bench) decision deals with a technical but important procedural question: when can a High Court suspend a criminal sentence and release a convicted person on bail while their case is pending before the Supreme Court?

The relevant law is Section 426(2B) of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows a High Court to suspend a sentence and grant bail if a convicted person has been granted "special leave to appeal" against a sentence the High Court itself imposed or upheld. A Deputy Prosecutor General had objected to this provision being used, apparently confusing "special leave to appeal" with a "certificate" that a High Court can issue confirming a case is fit for appeal to the Supreme Court.

The court clarified that these are two entirely different things. "Special leave to appeal" (now called "leave to appeal") can only be granted by the Supreme Court itself, under its constitutional and procedural powers—no High Court has authority to grant it. A High Court can only certify that a case involves a substantial legal question, which is a separate mechanism under Article 185 of the Constitution. The court traced the history of these provisions through the Constitution and Supreme Court Rules to support its reasoning.

Having clarified this distinction, the court overruled the prosecutor's objection, confirming that once the Supreme Court grants leave to appeal, the High Court retains power under Section 426(2B) to suspend the sentence and grant bail pending that appeal. This clarifies procedural rights for convicts awaiting Supreme Court appeals.

title: The base of Khula is verse 229 of Surah Al Baqrah
explainer:
This case is from the Azad Jammu and Kashmir High Court, deciding an appeal about a divorce dispute between a husband and wife. The wife had filed for dissolution of her marriage on grounds of cruelty, mental torture, non-payment of maintenance, and khula (a wife's Islamic right to seek separation from her husband). The husband opposed this and filed his own suit demanding restitution of conjugal rights, insisting his wife return to him. He also claimed that if khula were granted, his wife should return gold jewelry, household items, and dower money he had given her.

The trial court (Family Court, Mirpur) had already ruled in the wife's favor, granting the divorce through khula and dismissing the husband's case for restitution of conjugal rights. The husband appealed this decision to the High Court.

The High Court explained the Islamic legal basis for khula, tracing it to verse 229 of Surah Al-Baqarah in the Quran. It held that before granting khula, a court must be satisfied that the spouses cannot realistically continue their marriage happily within the moral and religious limits set by Islamic teaching, that the wife genuinely wants separation, and that she is willing to return consideration (such as dower) as required. Whether reconciliation is possible is a factual question depending on each case's circumstances.

This judgment is significant because it clarifies the religious and legal reasoning courts must apply when deciding khula cases, emphasizing that such decisions require careful factual assessment rather than automatic grants or refusals.

title: Khula is Islamic Right of a wife
explainer:
This case involved a husband challenging a court decision that granted his wife a divorce through khula, an Islamic legal mechanism allowing a wife to end her marriage. The wife had earlier filed a similar suit that was withdrawn after the couple reconciled and agreed to live together again, but the marriage broke down once more due to alleged mistreatment, so she filed a fresh suit. The trial court dissolved the marriage on condition she return the dower she had received.

The husband argued the second suit should not have been allowed since the first was withdrawn due to compromise, and also argued that the law allowing courts to grant khula without full evidence violated Islamic principles and his right to a fair trial.

The Lahore High Court rejected both arguments. It held that rules under the Civil Procedure Code barring repeat suits after withdrawal do not apply to family court cases, and that the wife's claims of renewed cruelty and hatred created a new cause of action, making her second suit valid. The court also held that khula is rooted in Quranic teaching, and that forcing spouses to remain in a hateful marriage causes social harm. If a wife firmly states she cannot maintain the marriage within God's limits, courts may accept this and dissolve the marriage. The petition was dismissed, upholding the wife's divorce and affirming khula as a legitimate Islamic right exercised through the family courts.
