title: Re-Examination of Witness under Article 133
explainer: This case from the Peshawar High Court dealt with a procedural error made by a trial court during a civil suit. A witness, Muhammad Zahid, had already testified before the court and been recorded as PW-10 (plaintiff's witness number 10). During his testimony, he mentioned a time as 11 o'clock, but the plaintiff later applied to correct this to 9 o'clock, claiming it was a clerical mistake. Instead of properly correcting or re-examining the existing witness, the trial court ordered that the same person be examined again, but this time as a "Court witness" (CW), along with recording the statement of a court stenographer. This was the second time this same case had come before the High Court due to similar mistakes by the trial court. The High Court explained that under the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (Pakistan's law of evidence), a witness who has already testified can only be re-examined under Article 133, not treated as a fresh "Court witness," since there is no legal provision allowing this. The High Court set aside the trial court's order as unlawful, but allowed the trial court to re-examine the witness properly under Article 133, giving the opposing party the right to cross-examine him. The case was sent back to the trial court with these instructions. This judgment clarifies correct procedure for re-examining witnesses and correcting testimony errors in Pakistani civil trials.

title: Re-Examination in Grievance Petition
explainer:
This case comes from the Punjab Labour Appellate Tribunal in Lahore, dealing with a dispute between the WASA/FDA administration in Faisalabad and an employee, Farukh Sagheer, who had filed a grievance petition under the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969.

During proceedings before the Labour Court, the employer's side asked to have its own witness recalled for re-examination, claiming the witness had made errors in his earlier statement that needed correction, and also wanted to bring in additional evidence. The Labour Court refused this request, and the employer challenged that refusal before the Appellate Tribunal.

The Tribunal upheld the Labour Court's decision and dismissed the petition. It explained that while the law does allow for additional evidence on appeal or re-examination of witnesses at trial, these are exceptional tools meant to help courts reach a fair and correct decision, not routine options for a party to fix its own mistakes or strengthen a weak case after the fact. Such requests are appropriate only when genuinely new and relevant evidence emerges, or when the court itself needs clarification. Here, the employer had already closed its evidence and made the request very late, after final arguments had been presented twice, with no good explanation.

The judgment matters because it reinforces the principle that court proceedings must have finality and integrity: parties cannot repeatedly reopen cases to reshape testimony in their favor, as this would undermine fairness to the opposing side and the trustworthiness of the judicial process.

title: Contract for Construction of Road Cancelled
explainer:
This case involved a road construction contract awarded by the Government of Punjab to a private contractor in 1993. After the contractor completed 60% of the work, the contract was cancelled. An arbitration award later found the contractor entitled to recover money from the Punjab government, and this award was made a court decree. While recovery proceedings were ongoing, the road in question was transferred to the National Highway Authority (NHA), a federal body. The executing court then ordered NHA to pay the decree amount, reasoning this was based on minutes of a meeting between the parties, and a civil revision against this order was also dismissed.

NHA challenged both orders before the Lahore High Court, arguing that under Section 10(2)(XV) of the National Highway Authority Act, 1991, roads transferred to it were meant to be handed over free of cost and without any liabilities or conditions. NHA argued the lower courts’ orders ignored this legal provision and wrongly relied on meeting minutes that could not override the law.

The High Court agreed with NHA, ruling that any decision or contract that contravenes a mandatory legal provision is void from the start and unenforceable, regardless of how much time has passed. Since the orders violated the NHA Act, they were nullities against which no limitation period could apply. The Court held that liability for the contractor’s claim could not be shifted onto NHA and set aside the lower courts’ orders. This case reinforces that courts must follow statutory law over informal arrangements, and that illegal orders can be challenged at any time.

title: Computing Sale Price of Acquired Land
explainer:
This case concerns compensation for land acquired by the National Highway Authority to build an additional carriageway on Multan Road, near Kasur. The government acquired land belonging to the appellants and initially valued it at a low rate, also awarding some compensation for damages and loss of goodwill related to a petrol pump and service station on the land. Dissatisfied, the landowners sought a review, and a Referee Court significantly increased the compensation rate and the damages awarded. However, when the matter went to the Lahore High Court, it reduced the compensation again, relying mainly on a single sale instance found in revenue records, and largely ignored the issue of damages.

The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's approach. It held that compensation for acquired land must reflect not just past sale prices but broader factors such as the land's location, its potential future use, and how neighbouring land was being used. The Referee Court had properly considered average sale prices of comparable commercial land, while the High Court relied on just one sale and failed to properly address the damages issue, even though the acquiring authority itself had admitted losses were suffered.

The Supreme Court therefore set aside the High Court's judgment and restored the Referee Court's earlier decision granting higher compensation and damages. This case matters because it clarifies how courts should fairly calculate compensation for land acquired by the state, ensuring landowners are not shortchanged and that broader market and potential-use factors are properly considered.

title: Case Regarding Violation of Modesty
explainer:
This case involved a woman, Ayesha Bibi, who had filed criminal cases against a man (Respondent No. 2), including one alleging violation of her modesty and another for assault and theft of her gold ornaments. In response, the man filed a civil suit for damages and then a private criminal complaint accusing her of defamation under Section 500 of the Pakistan Penal Code, claiming her criminal complaints had damaged his reputation. When police refused to register a defamation case against her, he pursued it through the courts, which took up his complaint. The woman tried to get the case dismissed early under Section 265-K of the Criminal Procedure Code, arguing it was merely retaliation and blackmail, but lower courts and the High Court rejected her request.

The Supreme Court examined whether someone can be sued for defamation simply for filing a criminal complaint or giving information to police. It held that such complainants generally enjoy immunity, because effective policing depends on people feeling safe to report crimes without fear of being sued for defamation afterward. Using defamation claims to punish those who report crimes would undermine the justice system and amount to abuse of court process. The Court noted the proper remedy for false or malicious complaints is a claim of malicious prosecution under Section 250 of the Criminal Procedure Code, not defamation.

This ruling matters because it protects citizens who report crimes, including victims of assault, from being harassed through retaliatory defamation lawsuits, reinforcing public confidence in reporting wrongdoing.

title: Legal Value of Talak-e-Tafweez
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a husband, Sajid Hussain Tanoli, and his wife, Nadia Khattak, after their marriage broke down. The wife filed a family court suit seeking maintenance for their daughter and recovery of dower money, claiming she had exercised her delegated right to divorce herself (called talaq-e-tafweez) because of the husband's cruelty. This right had been written into their marriage contract (Nikah Nama), which allowed her to divorce herself under certain conditions. The husband denied ever granting this power and argued that even if it existed, it should be treated as khula (a wife seeking divorce through court), not a true talaq, meaning she should not get dower.

The trial court and appellate court ruled largely in the wife's favor, granting dower and maintenance while making some adjustments. The husband challenged these decisions before the Peshawar High Court.

The High Court upheld that the husband had indeed delegated divorce power to his wife through the Nikah Nama, and this was proven through evidence including his own admissions. The court clarified that talaq-e-tafweez is legally distinct from khula: with tafweez, the wife herself can pronounce divorce without needing the husband's or court's consent, whereas khula requires seeking dissolution from the husband or court. Once exercised, such delegated divorce becomes irrevocable and is treated as if the husband himself pronounced it.

title: Even evidence of a single person is sufficient for conviction
explainer:
This case concerns an appeal against a murder conviction. The appellant, Muhammad Waseem Khan, had been sentenced to death by a trial court for stabbing Ibrar Hussain to death outside a courthouse in Rawalpindi in 2008. According to the prosecution, the killing arose from a grudge connected to an earlier abduction case involving the deceased and a woman named Mst. Gultaj Bibi. The complainant, the deceased's brother, said he witnessed the attack firsthand.

The defense argued that the conviction relied too heavily on a single witness who was the deceased's brother and therefore potentially biased, and that the prosecution had failed to produce another key witness (the appellant's own mother, who had been listed but later dropped as a witness).

The Lahore High Court upheld the conviction, ruling that the testimony of even one witness can be enough to convict someone if that testimony is truthful, consistent, and not shown to be driven by hostility or self-interest. The court found the brother's account credible and unshaken, and accepted the prosecution's explanation for why the mother was not called to testify (she had remarried the deceased and, having lost two husbands to violence, was unwilling to testify against her son).

However, the court did reduce the sentence, taking into account the appellant's young age at the time (19 years) and the underlying provocation, showing that Pakistani courts can adjust punishment even while affirming guilt.

title: Dower Amount paid can be restored to Husband
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a wife and husband after their marriage ended in khula, a form of divorce initiated by the wife. Shortly after marrying, the wife sued for dissolution of marriage, return of dowry articles, and maintenance. The trial court dissolved the marriage through khula, finding she had not proven cruelty by her husband, and denied her maintenance since the marriage had never been consummated and this was not the husband's fault. It also ordered return of her dowry articles but initially did not require her to return gold ornaments given at the time of rukhsati (the formal start of married life), since the husband had not specifically asked for their return. On appeal, the appellate court ordered the wife to return the five tolas of gold. Both parties then challenged the decisions before the Peshawar High Court.

The High Court upheld the khula divorce, finding the wife had shown she could not live within the limits prescribed by God, even though she hadn't proven cruelty or impotence. It also upheld the husband's right to recover the gold ornaments, since the wife herself admitted taking them when she left. The court explained that when a wife seeks khula without fault on the husband's part, it is fair for the husband to be repaid what he gave as dower, though he should not claim more than that. This case matters because it clarifies that in khula cases, courts can restore dower to the husband even without an explicit claim, balancing fairness to both spouses.

title: Muslim Family Law has Overriding Effect Over General Law

The couple married in 2008 but never lived together (no rukhsati), and the husband, a Canadian resident, later withdrew his sponsorship of her immigration visa. He then sent a divorce notice on stamp paper to the local Union Council. The wife, during reconciliation proceedings, admitted receiving the divorce notice but demanded that divorce be processed through Canadian law along with payment of her dower and maintenance before any certificate was issued. The husband did not appoint an arbitrator but confirmed the divorce in a notarized letter from Canada. The Union Council eventually issued a certificate confirming the divorce had taken effect, and the wife challenged this in court, arguing procedural requirements under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance were not properly followed.

The court dismissed her petition, holding that since she had never denied receiving the divorce notice, technical evidentiary objections did not apply. title: PLJ 2018 Islamabad 239
explainer:
This case concerns a challenge to a government notification that limited where Pakistan's rent control law applies within Islamabad. Two advocates filed a public interest petition arguing that SRO No. 83(K)/2002, issued in 2002, excluded about 60 percent of the Islamabad Capital Territory, including many residential, institutional and industrial areas developed by the Capital Development Authority, from the protection of the Islamabad Rent Restriction Ordinance, 2001. This meant landlords and tenants in large parts of the city, including Zone-V, had no access to the rent control protections available elsewhere in Islamabad.

The Islamabad High Court held that the notification was arbitrary and lacked any reasonable justification or intelligible differentia for excluding these areas, making it discriminatory and a violation of citizens' fundamental rights to equality before law and equal protection of law under Articles 4 and 25 of the Constitution. The court emphasized that anyone can challenge a law or notification to protect fundamental rights, and that High Courts have wide power under Article 199 to strike down unconstitutional government actions and issue directions, including a writ of mandamus, compelling authorities to perform their legal duties.

The court ruled that the Federal Government must reconsider and amend the notification to include the excluded areas, since it retains power under the General Clauses Act to amend its own orders. The petition was allowed, reinforcing that government regulations must be fair, reasoned, and non-discriminatory.

title: PLJ 2018 Cr.C. (Islamabad) 83
explainer:
This case involved three men convicted of robbing Bank Alfalah's Sabzi Mandi branch in Islamabad, where armed gunmen made off with over Rs. 3.8 million. They were sentenced to seven years under Section 395 (dacoity) and three years under Section 412 of the Pakistan Penal Code, plus fines, by the trial court.

On appeal, the Islamabad High Court found serious flaws in how the case was handled. Most importantly, no proper charge under Sections 395/412 PPC had ever actually been framed against the accused. The original charge was only under a Hudood Ordinance provision (Section 17, dealing with Harabah), which was later deleted by a different judge, but the trial court never framed a fresh, correct charge before convicting the men.

The conviction also relied heavily on an identification parade, but the two eyewitnesses who were supposed to have identified the accused during that parade were never even produced in court, and no witness confirmed identifying the appellants at trial. CCTV footage that could have supported the case was also never produced as evidence.

The High Court concluded there was essentially no valid evidence against the appellants. Rather than sending the case back for a retrial, the court decided that doing so would be pointless since the fundamental evidence gaps could not be fixed. The appeal was allowed, meaning the convictions were overturned. The case highlights the importance of properly framing charges and presenting genuine evidence before someone can be convicted of a serious crime.

title: Admission must be clear, specific and unambiguous
explainer:
This Sindh High Court judgment arose from three related civil suits between Media Max (Pvt.) Ltd. and ARY Communication (Pvt.) Ltd., apparently involving disputes over a commercial or agency arrangement, requests for injunctions, appointment of a receiver, and contempt allegations.

The judge, Justice Muhammad Ali Mazhar, addressed several important procedural and legal principles rather than deciding the underlying commercial dispute on its merits. On injunctions, the court held that it retains full power to vary, modify or discharge a stay order if circumstances change after it was issued. On agency law, the court explained when an agent's authority becomes irrevocable because it is coupled with an interest, clarifying that merely expecting a commission does not create such an interest. Regarding contempt of court, the judge stressed that before framing a formal contempt charge, the court must first satisfy itself that a prima facie case exists. On receivers, the court explained that appointing a receiver is a harsh, discretionary remedy requiring a strong prima facie case of title and risk of harm to the property, distinguishing it from the lower threshold needed for a temporary injunction. Finally, on rejecting a plaint, the court reiterated that only the plaintiff's own pleadings can be examined, and weak evidence is not grounds for rejection—only a fundamentally defective or legally barred claim justifies dismissal at that stage.

This judgment matters because it consolidates and clarifies important civil procedure principles used routinely in Pakistani

title: Successive Bail Petitions
explainer:
This is a Supreme Court of Pakistan order dealing with a bail matter that had been repeatedly filed and withdrawn before the Lahore High Court, Multan Bench.

The petitioner, Rizwan Ali, had filed successive bail applications before the High Court, but each time the application was withdrawn without the High Court actually examining the merits of his case for bail. When his most recent bail application was disposed of on 19 June 2013, he approached the Supreme Court, arguing that the High Court had not properly applied the legal principles set out in earlier Supreme Court decisions (Muhammad Siddique v. The State and Amir Masih v. The State, 2013 SCMR 1059) regarding how such bail matters should be handled.

At the hearing, the petitioner's counsel, the state's prosecutor, and the complainant all agreed that the High Court had indeed failed to correctly apply these principles and had never actually considered the substance of Rizwan Ali's bail request- each prior withdrawal was simply a withdrawal, not a decision on merits.

Given this agreement among all parties, the Supreme Court converted the petition into an appeal, allowed it, set aside the High Court's order, and sent the bail application back to the High Court. The High Court was directed to decide the bail application afresh, this time actually examining the merits of the petitioner's case, rather than allowing it to be withdrawn again without proper consideration.

title: Procedure when accused is of unsound mind
explainer:
This case concerns whether a man accused of murder, who claimed to be mentally unsound, should be granted bail while the question of his mental fitness to stand trial remained undecided.

Farooque Tayyab Imrani was accused of shooting Muhammad Yaqub dead in a mosque in Karachi in 1989 and was charged with murder. His lawyers raised the issue that he might be of unsound mind and unable to defend himself, and asked the trial court to hold a medical inquiry, as required under sections 464 and 465 of the Criminal Procedure Code. This inquiry process dragged on for nearly two years, moving between different judges, with doctors eventually testifying about his mental condition. Before the inquiry was completed, the Sessions Judge granted him interim bail, which was later confirmed.

The victim's son challenged this, asking the Sindh High Court to cancel the bail, arguing that proper procedure under sections 464, 465 and 466 had not been followed.

The High Court explained that these sections apply when an accused becomes of unsound mind during trial, not at the time of the offence, and require a court's tentative satisfaction of incapacity before triggering the formal inquiry process. Although the lower courts had not strictly followed this procedure, the High Court found that the accused qualified as a "sick person" under section 497(1) of the Cr.P.C., which allows bail on medical grounds. The court therefore dismissed the application to cancel his bail.

The case clarifies how courts should handle bail and procedural safeguards for accused persons

title: Bail Allowed as FIR was lodge after one year Delay
explainer:
This case involves a bail petition heard by the Lahore High Court. The petitioner, Muhammad Asif, was accused under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with issuing a cheque that bounces despite knowing there were insufficient funds. The complainant alleged that Asif issued a cheque worth Rs. 10 lakh that was dishonoured when presented to the bank. However, the FIR was only lodged more than a year after the alleged offence, and this delay was never explained by the prosecution.

The court noted several important points in granting bail. First, the offence carries a maximum punishment of three years, meaning it does not fall under the more serious category of offences where bail is typically harder to get. Second, whether the cheque was issued dishonestly is a matter to be decided at trial, not at the bail stage. Third, the court emphasized that Section 489-F is meant to be a criminal provision, not a tool for recovering unpaid debts. The court also noted that although Asif faced similar cases elsewhere, he had been granted bail in all of them and was not convicted in any. Since the investigation was complete and the trial had not yet begun, the court found no benefit in keeping him in custody indefinitely, granting him bail with financial sureties.

title: Appointment of Counsel at State Expense
explainer:
This case comes from the Lahore High Court and concerns a murder trial where the complainant, Muhammad Adnan, challenged a lower court's decision to allow re-examination of prosecution witnesses.

During the trial, one of the accused failed to hire a private lawyer, so the trial court appointed a defence counsel for him at state expense. This state-appointed lawyer cross-examined several witnesses, including two key eyewitnesses. Months later, after finally engaging his own private lawyer, the accused asked the trial court to recall these already-cross-examined witnesses so his new counsel could question them again. The trial court partially agreed, allowing two of the witnesses to be recalled.

The complainant challenged this in the High Court, arguing that witnesses who had already gone through cross-examination should not be repeatedly summoned just because the accused later hired a different lawyer.

The High Court agreed with the complainant. It held that simply switching from a state-appointed lawyer to a private one is not sufficient grounds to reopen completed cross-examinations, especially when the accused could not show he had actually been prejudiced or disadvantaged by the earlier cross-examination. The court emphasized that the law allowing additional evidence or recalling witnesses cannot be used to fill gaps in the defence's strategy, and that witnesses should not be forced to keep returning to court without genuine cause. The trial court's order was set aside, and the case was sent back to continue without re-examining the witnesses, with instructions to conclude the long-pending trial within two months. title: There is no limitation for Order IX Rule 7 Petition
explainer:
This case is about a man who was sued for a house dispute and money recovery of Rs. 500,000. During the trial, he stopped appearing in court, so proceedings continued without him (ex parte), and the court eventually decided the case against him. He later tried to get that decision overturned, but both the trial court and the appellate court rejected his request, saying he had filed too late.

He then approached the Peshawar High Court, arguing that since the law does not set a specific time limit for challenging ex parte proceedings, he should get three years under a general provision of the Limitation Act.

The High Court disagreed. It clarified that once a court has proceeded ex parte and gone on to decide the case, a defendant cannot ask that same court to undo the ex parte order under Rule 7 of Order IX of the Civil Procedure Code, because that rule only applies before or at the hearing when the case is adjourned ex parte, not after a decree has already been passed. Once a decree is passed, the only remedies are to apply under Order IX Rule 13 (with a 30-day limit) or file a regular appeal. Since the man had been properly served with court summons throughout, and had actively participated for much of the case, his very late application could not be excused. The court upheld the dismissal of his petition, reinforcing clear time limits for challenging ex parte decrees.

title: Ingredients of valid gift according to Muhammadan Law
explainer:
This case involved a dispute among stepbrothers and sisters over land left by their late father, Allah Bakhash. Some of the children (the plaintiffs) challenged a mutation entered in 2001 that recorded a gift supposedly made by their father in favor of the petitioners, who received the largest share of the property. The plaintiffs argued the gift was fraudulent, made when their father was seriously ill with cancer, bedridden, and largely unconscious for about three years before his death, and that it was designed to cut them out of their rightful inheritance.

The trial court and the appellate court both ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, cancelling the gift mutation. The matter then came before the Lahore High Court (Multan Bench) through a civil revision petition filed by the beneficiaries of the gift.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions. It found that basic requirements of a valid gift under Muhammadan Law—offer, acceptance, and proof that the gift was free of undue influence—were missing. Notably, the gift document did not bear the signatures or thumb impressions of the other heirs, and evidence showed the father was gravely ill and mentally impaired when the gift was allegedly made. The court also noted the suspicious nature of a dying man disinheriting his other children.

The case reaffirms that gifts made by seriously ill or mentally incapacitated persons, especially those excluding rightful heirs, must meet strict legal requirements and can be struck down if fraud or undue influence is shown.

title: Judgment on cancellation of PHD Degree
explainer:
This case involved a former Assistant Professor at Allama Iqbal Open University who had earned a PhD, only to have his degree cancelled by the university a short time after it was awarded. He challenged the cancellation in court, arguing the university had acted out of bad faith, lacked the legal power to revoke the degree, and that the decision was based on technical or procedural issues rather than any real problem with the academic quality of his thesis, especially since there was no allegation of plagiarism. His civil suit was dismissed, and this outcome was upheld by two lower courts before reaching the Supreme Court of Pakistan.

The Supreme Court noted that leave to appeal had originally been granted because the university appeared not to have followed proper procedure, such as issuing a show-cause notice before cancelling the degree, violating the basic principle that no one should be penalized without being heard. However, after hearing arguments, the Court declined to send the thesis for fresh evaluation, since this specific request had not been part of his original court petition and courts generally do not add new relief that was never pleaded. The Court also emphasized that since three previous courts had already agreed on the outcome, it would not disturb these consistent findings.

While upholding the cancellation of the PhD degree, the Supreme Court did order that any adverse remarks made against the appellant's personal integrity by the lower courts be removed, recognizing his otherwise strong academic record and that the procedural problems appeared linked to conduct by university officials, not misconduct by him.

title: Judgment on Jurisdiction of Rent Controller
citation: PLD 1969 SC 187 The State v. Muhammad Jamil and Muhammad Alam v. The
explainer:
This case dealt with a landlord tenant dispute over a shop in the F-6/1 Shopping Center in Islamabad. The landlords filed an eviction case against the tenant on 29 January 2003, claiming he had defaulted on rent payments. The Rent Controller ordered eviction, and this was upheld on appeal and then by the Islamabad High Court.

The tenant challenged the case on a technical ground: he argued that the Rent Controller had no legal authority to hear the eviction case in 2003, because the notification actually extending the Rent Controller's jurisdiction over that area was only issued later, on 29 June 2004. Since the case had already been filed before that date, he claimed it should never have been entertained.

The Supreme Court rejected this argument. It explained that when a court or tribunal lacks jurisdiction at the time a case is filed but later acquires it while the case is still pending, it can validly decide the matter using its newly acquired jurisdiction. Since the shop fell within the area later covered by the 2004 notification, and the case was still pending when that notification came into effect, the Rent Controller's decision was valid.

The Court also rejected the tenant's separate claim that he was not actually in possession of the property, finding evidence showed otherwise. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, upholding the eviction order. The case clarifies an important principle: jurisdiction acquired during a pending case can validly apply retroactively to that case.

title: Setting aside of Ex-Parte Decree
explainer:
This case involved a long-running dispute over land in Mauza Kaskalyal, Mirpur, that went through multiple rounds of litigation. It began with a 1990 consent decree between two parties over shared (Shamlat Deh) land. Later, others challenged that decree, leading to it being set aside in 1998. Still later, respondents Mushtaq Ahmed and another person, who claimed ownership through a 1991 sale deed, applied to have that 1998 decision set aside as well, arguing they were never made parties to the earlier case even though officials knew about their claim. The trial court accepted their application in 2008, prompting the current petitioners, who claimed to be the actual owners in possession of the land, to challenge that decision before the Azad Kashmir High Court.

The High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners, setting aside the trial court's order. It found that the respondents had failed to prove their case, that their application was time-barred, and that they had been negligent in pursuing their rights for years, which does not count as a valid excuse for delay. The court also held that since the petitioners were in actual possession of the land but had never been made parties to the original suit, the consent decree and the sale deed based on it were not legally binding on them.

This case matters because it clarifies the limits on setting aside ex parte decrees, emphasizing that courts must properly implead all necessary parties, especially those in possession of disputed property, and that delay caused by a party's own negligence cannot justify reopening old decisions.

title: Nawaz Shareef Election Case
explainer:
This case involved a legal dispute over whether Mian Muhammad Nawaz Sharif could contest elections for the National Assembly, following his earlier conviction and sentencing by an Anti-Terrorism Court. Although the President had pardoned his sentence, the underlying conviction had not been overturned by any appellate court, raising questions about his eligibility under election laws. Separately, and central to much of the judgment, the case examined whether certain Supreme Court judges should recuse themselves from hearing the matter due to allegations of bias, given disputes about the judges' own appointments and the political controversy surrounding them.

The Supreme Court held that judges cannot be disqualified from adjudicating simply because litigants make broad, undifferentiated allegations against the entire judiciary. It emphasized that a litigant who has already accepted a judge's authority and participated in proceedings cannot later demand recusal as a tactic, and that unfounded claims of bias should not be allowed to obstruct the administration of justice. The Court also addressed procedural questions, ruling that a candidate's proposer and seconder could not independently contest the candidate's disqualification if the candidate himself chose not to defend his own qualifications before the Election Tribunal.

This judgment matters because it clarifies principles about judicial impartiality, the limits of recusal demands, and who has legal standing to contest election disqualifications, reinforcing that personal electoral disputes must generally be defended by the candidate themselves.

title: Re-Examination in case of further evidence
explainer:
This case involved a group of accused persons who were charged by the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) with collecting large sums of money from people wanting to perform Hajj, then misappropriating the funds instead of arranging the pilgrimage as promised. After the prosecution finished presenting its evidence at trial, the accused asked the Accountability Court to summon 33 witnesses as defence witnesses, even though these same witnesses had already been examined and cross-examined by the prosecution. The trial court refused this request, but the Peshawar High Court overturned that refusal, holding that the accused had an unqualified right to recall and re-examine any prosecution witness as a defence witness.

The Supreme Court disagreed and allowed the NAB Chairman's appeal. It clarified that witnesses summoned by a court under Section 540 of the Criminal Procedure Code are court witnesses, not witnesses belonging to either the prosecution or the defence, so neither side can claim an automatic right to recall them. Such witnesses may only be recalled if the court itself believes their further evidence is genuinely necessary to reach a just decision, not simply because a party requests it. The judgment also stressed that courts have a duty to protect witnesses from unnecessary harassment and repeated examination, and that judges must apply the correct law themselves rather than defer to what counsel or parties argue. This ruling matters because it limits misuse of witness-recall provisions to delay or complicate trials, particularly in accountability and financial crime cases.

title: PLJ 2015 Lahore 970
explainer:
This case from the Lahore High Court dealt with a dispute over how a Muslim woman should exercise a delegated right of divorce under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961. The couple had married under Shia personal law, and the wife, using divorce powers delegated to her in the marriage contract (nikahnama), issued a divorce and sent notice to the union council where the marriage had been registered. The husband challenged this, arguing that the notice should instead have gone to the union council located where the wife actually resided, and also argued that under Shia law (Fiqa-e-Jafferia) a divorce is only valid if specific Arabic words (Segheas) are recited in the presence of both parties.

The court ruled against the husband. It held that since the union council where a marriage is registered is generally the one covering the bride's residence, sending the divorce notice there was proper. It also found that the required religious formalities had in fact been completed, as certified by an Islamic scholarly board, satisfying Shia law requirements. The judge emphasized that Shia personal law on divorce is not so rigid that a woman remains permanently dependent on her husband's cooperation to obtain a valid divorce.

This case matters because it clarifies procedural requirements for women exercising delegated divorce rights and affirms that family law should be interpreted in a way that protects women's ability to exit marriages, rather than creating technical obstacles that trap them.

title: PLJ 2018 Lahore 646 (FB)
explainer:
This case concerns a legal challenge by City School (Private) Limited against a Punjab government law regulating fees charged by private educational institutions. The government had amended the Punjab Private Educational Institutions Ordinance, 1984 by inserting Section 7-A, which capped annual fee increases at 5 percent (later raised to 8 percent), with the stated aim of preventing commercialization and profiteering in private education. The petitioner argued this violated its constitutional right under Article 18 to freely conduct trade and business, claiming the fee cap was an unreasonable restriction.

The Lahore High Court's Full Bench rejected this challenge and upheld the fee-capping provision. The court reasoned that the right to conduct trade or business under Article 18 is not absolute and can be reasonably regulated by law, especially through licensing systems like the one governing private schools, which must register and follow rules to operate. The court also emphasized that education is closely tied to the fundamental right to life and dignity, and after the 18th Constitutional Amendment, is itself an independent fundamental right under Article 25-A. It found that regulating school fees was a legitimate and reasonable exercise of the state's regulatory power, especially since fee regulation already existed before the amendment.

This judgment matters because it affirms the government's authority to regulate private school fees in the public interest, balancing business freedom against the fundamental right to accessible education.

title: Pecuniary Jurisdiction in case of confiscated vehicle
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over smuggled iron and steel scrap intercepted by Customs officials near Quetta in 2004. Three trucks carrying the scrap were stopped, and since the drivers could not produce import documents, the goods were seized. A committee later confirmed the scrap was of foreign origin, and a Deputy Collector ordered confiscation of both the scrap and the vehicles used to transport it, while giving vehicle owners the option to pay a fine to redeem their vehicles.

The vehicle owners appealed, and the Collector (Appeal) allowed release of the vehicles on payment of a redemption fine. Separately, the Customs Appellate Tribunal later set aside the original confiscation order. This raised a legal question: did setting aside the original order automatically cancel the earlier appellate order releasing the vehicles?

The key legal issue was jurisdiction. At the relevant time, a Single Member of the Appellate Tribunal could only hear cases where the value of goods was up to Rs. 200,000, though this limit was later raised to Rs. 500,000. Since the scrap involved was valued at over Rs. 500,000, the Court found that the Single Member did not have jurisdiction to decide the matter, and the later increase in the limit could not be applied retroactively to fix this defect.

title: Illegal Selling of Auqaf Properties
explainer: The Supreme Court took up this matter on its own initiative (suo motu) after concerns were raised about a land deal between the Evacuee Trust Property Board (ETP Board) and the Defence Housing Authority (DHA). The ETP Board had originally agreed to exchange evacuee trust land with DHA in return for 33% of the resulting developed plots. But after the Board was reconstituted and a new chairman appointed, that deal was quietly revised down to just 25% - even though DHA's own offer had actually improved in the meantime. The Court found this reduction suspicious, noting it caused real financial loss to a charitable trust and appeared to reflect improper motives behind the Board's reconstitution. It ruled the revised 25% agreement unlawful, and gave DHA a choice: honor the original, better 33% terms within 30 days, or return the entire property. The case is a clear example of the Court using its suo motu power to step in and protect public/charitable assets from being quietly given away below their fair value.

title: Civil Court Cannot Be Rent Controller
explainer: This case addresses a common practical problem: what happens when a landlord and tenant end up fighting the same property dispute in two different forums at once - a regular civil suit and a separate rent case? Here, one side had filed a civil suit for specific performance based on a lease agreement, while the other side filed ejectment (eviction) cases over the same property. The petitioner asked the trial court to consolidate all these cases together to avoid contradictory rulings, but the request was denied. The Islamabad High Court held that this refusal was correct in principle: a Rent Controller and a Civil Court operate under different procedures and different laws (the Rent Ordinance vs. the Civil Procedure Code), so their cases generally shouldn't be merged just because they involve the same property. That said, the Court still allowed the petitioner's revision, finding room within the specific facts of this case to proceed differently. The core takeaway for practitioners: rent matters and civil suits are legally distinct tracks, even when they arise from the same underlying property dispute.

title: Bridal Gift is not returnable
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

A husband (Shah Nawaz) and wife (Suria Bibi) were in a legal dispute after their marriage broke down. The wife had sued for maintenance, dower (mahr), a share in property, and dissolution of marriage. She had received 10 tolas of gold ornaments and 5 kanals of land as dower under a deed signed at marriage.

The trial court initially ordered the return of conjugal rights to the husband and awarded gold to the wife. On appeal, the Additional District Judge granted the wife a divorce through *Khula* (a wife-initiated divorce), on the condition that she give up her claim to the 5 kanals of land. However, the appellate court still allowed her to keep the 10 tolas of gold, treating it now as a "bridal gift" rather than dower.

The husband challenged this in the Peshawar High Court, arguing that under the Bridal Gift Act, 1976, she wasn't entitled to keep the gold.

**What did the court decide?**

The High Court dismissed the husband's petition. It ruled that once a couple marries, signs the dower deed, and lives together as husband and wife, the husband is legally bound to give the promised gifts/dower — and the Bridal Gift Act's restrictions don't apply to cancel this obligation.

**Why it matters:**
This case clarifies that marital gifts or dower promised in a deed remain the wife's entitlement even after divorce, reinforcing protections for women's property rights within Islamic family law in Pakistan.

title: CPC and QSO are not applicable in family suits
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

A husband and wife were disputing dowry articles after their marriage broke down. The wife had filed a suit to recover dowry items (or their cash value) from her husband. The Family Court ruled largely in her favor, and this decision was upheld and even partly enhanced on appeal. The husband then challenged these decisions before the Lahore High Court, arguing about procedural issues—particularly whether certain documents and testimony (including a list of dowry items and statements given through his "special attorney") should have been considered as valid evidence.

**What did the court decide?**

The High Court dismissed the husband's objections. It clarified two important points:

1. Under family law, a husband can be represented by an attorney, and statements/written submissions made through that attorney are valid and can be considered by the court.
2. Ordinary civil procedure rules (the Code of Civil Procedure) and the standard law of evidence (Qanun-e-Shahadat) do **not** strictly apply in family court cases. Family Court judges have flexibility in how they handle evidence and procedure. Once a document is formally exhibited as evidence, it cannot later be "de-exhibited" or excluded on technical grounds.

**Why does this matter?**

This ruling reinforces that family courts operate with more flexible, simplified procedures than regular civil courts—prioritizing substantive justice over rigid technical rules. This makes it harder for parties to use procedural technicalities to delay or derail family disputes like dowry recovery cases, helping such cases be resolved more effic

title: Every muslim is sunni unless proved contrary
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

A woman, Mst. Sarwar Noor, claimed she was the sole heir to her deceased mother's land, arguing that because her mother was "Shia," a male relative (a collateral relative on her father's side) who would normally inherit under Sunni inheritance rules should be excluded. This claim mattered because Sunni and Shia inheritance rules differ, particularly regarding which relatives count as heirs.

However, she had never raised this "Shia" argument during the earlier revenue proceedings (mutation disputes, appeals, and a revision petition)—she only brought it up when she filed a fresh civil suit. The male relative, meanwhile, argued the family was actually Sunni.

**What did the court decide?**

The Lahore High Court dismissed her case. It held that Pakistani law presumes every Muslim is Sunni unless proven otherwise. Since she was claiming her mother was Shia (the exception), the burden was on her to prove it. Her only evidence was that a "Shia Maulvi" led the funeral prayers—which the court found weak and insufficient, especially since the opposing side produced an equal number of witnesses supporting the Sunni claim.

**Why does it matter?**

This case establishes an important legal presumption in Pakistani inheritance law: courts will assume a Muslim is Sunni by default, and anyone claiming otherwise (to invoke different inheritance rules) must provide strong, convincing proof—not just minor circumstantial details like who performed a funeral prayer.

title: Importance of columns of Nikahnama
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

A husband and wife married in 2005, but the "rukhsati" (the ceremony where the wife moves to the husband's home to start married life) never took place, and the marriage was never consummated. The husband eventually divorced her in 2007. The Nikahnama (marriage contract) contained several important entries: dower of Rs. 300,000 already paid at the time of Nikah, additional items (gold ornaments and a house) promised at the time of rukhsati, and a special condition that if the husband ever divorced her or remarried, he would pay an extra Rs. 200,000. The wife sued for the dower, this extra Rs. 200,000, and maintenance allowance.

**What did the courts decide?**

The Family Court and appellate court found that since rukhsati never occurred, she wasn't entitled to the deferred items. Courts also ruled the Family Court had no jurisdiction to enforce the special Rs. 200,000 penalty clause, since this didn't count as "personal property" under the law governing what Family Courts can decide. However, she was awarded maintenance from the date of Nikah until divorce, since the husband—not her—had caused the delay in rukhsati.

**Why it matters:**

This case clarifies that not everything written in a Nikahnama can automatically be enforced by Family Courts—only matters falling within their specific legal jurisdiction. It also confirms that a wife is entitled to maintenance even without rukhsati if the delay was the husband's fault.

title: Ipxi-Dixit of Police is not binding on courts
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

Muhammad Tufail was arrested and charged under Section 9(c) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, following an FIR registered in October 2009 after police intercepted a car allegedly used to transport narcotics. He applied to the Lahore High Court seeking post-arrest bail.

**What did the court find?**

The court noted that no one was actually caught in the car when it was stopped, and no witness testified that Tufail was driving it. Nothing was recovered from his direct personal possession. Although the police investigating officer later claimed (in a case diary) that Tufail was driving the car and was linked to the main suspect, the court held that such police opinions are not automatically binding — this is a well-established principle in criminal law. The claim would need to be tested at trial.

The court also pointed out that Tufail's co-accused, Muhammad Tariq, had already been granted bail by the same court in a similar situation, and there was nothing distinguishing Tufail's case from his. For consistency, similar accused persons should be treated similarly.

**Why does it matter?**

Considering Tufail had already spent months in custody and had no prior criminal record, the court granted him bail, subject to bail bonds of Rs. 500,000 with two sureties. The case reinforces two important legal principles: police statements/opinions alone don't bind courts, and courts should maintain consistency when treating co-accused in similar circumstances.

title: Judgement Related with State Bank Employees Pension Matters
explainer:
This case is about employees of the State Bank of Pakistan who voluntarily left their jobs under a 1997 "Golden Handshake" scheme designed to reduce surplus staff. Under this scheme, employees who opted in received compensation equal to 50% commutation of their gross pension, as a full and final settlement — a special, one-time arrangement, not the regular pension system.

About 1400 employees accepted this deal. Six years later, some of them went to court seeking additional pensionary benefits (a regular monthly pension) on top of what they'd already received, arguing they should get the same benefits as employees who retired normally after serving 25 years or reaching age 60. The High Court of Sindh ruled in their favor, ordering the Bank to pay pension benefits regardless of the scheme's terms.

The State Bank appealed to the Supreme Court, which reversed the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court held that the employees had voluntarily chosen the scheme, understood its terms in advance, and accepted a special one-time payout instead of regular pension. Since they hadn't completed 25 years of service, they weren't entitled to normal retirement pension. The Court also found the employees waited too long (six years) to complain, which barred their claim under the legal principle of "laches" (unreasonable delay defeats a claim).

This case matters because it clarifies that voluntary settlement schemes are binding once accepted, and employees cannot later demand additional benefits beyond what was agreed, especially after long delays.

title: Muslim Family Law Ordinance is not applicable on non muslims
explainer:
This case addressed whether Family Courts in Pakistan have jurisdiction to hear family disputes—like maintenance, dowry, and divorce—involving non-Muslims, specifically members of the Ahmadi community (whom Pakistan's Constitution classifies as non-Muslim).

The petitioner, a husband being sued by his wife and others for maintenance, dower, dowry items, and divorce, argued that the Family Court had no jurisdiction because the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance (MFLO), 1961 only applies to Muslims, and since Ahmadis are constitutionally non-Muslim, they should instead use their own religious "Dar-ul-Qaza" system rather than state Family Courts.

The Lahore High Court rejected this argument. It held that the Family Courts Act, 1964 is "religion neutral" and was designed to handle personal law matters for people of all faiths, not just Muslims. The phrase "subject to the MFLO" in the Act only matters when there's an actual conflict between the two laws for Muslim litigants—it doesn't strip Family Courts of jurisdiction over non-Muslims. The MFLO itself explicitly applies only to Muslims. The court also noted that lack of a formally "codified" personal law (as with Ahmadi religious law) doesn't prevent Family Courts from hearing such cases.

The petition was dismissed, confirming that Family Courts can handle family disputes of non-Muslims, including Ahmadis, ensuring access to formal justice reg

# Case Explainer: Muhammad Yaqub v. Master Muhammad Shafi

**What was this case about?**

This was a landlord-tenant dispute over a house in Quetta. Under rent law, once eviction proceedings begin, the Rent Controller can order a tenant to keep depositing rent regularly. If the tenant fails to pay on time, the landlord can ask the court to "strike off" (cancel) the tenant's defence, which effectively leads to eviction.

Here, the tenant missed depositing rent for June 1980. The landlord found out and applied over a year later to have the tenant's defence struck off. The tenant argued that this long delay meant the landlord had "waived" (given up) his right to object, and separately claimed he was seriously ill when the delay occurred.

**What did the court decide?**

The court found the tenant had acted deceptively — depositing rent through court challans (receipts) without mentioning which month it was for, and even erasing/altering details to hide the missed payment. Because the landlord didn't know about the default earlier, he could not be said to have knowingly waived his right — waiver requires knowledge of a right and a deliberate decision to give it up. The illness excuse was also rejected as an afterthought, since it wasn't raised when the tenant first tendered the late rent.

The court upheld the order striking off the tenant's defence and eviction.

title: Power of a family court in khula cases
explainer:
This case involves a wife, Dr. Nosheen Qamar, who sued for dissolution of her marriage on grounds including cruelty, non-payment of maintenance, and her husband taking a second wife without her consent. She also claimed dower (money and property promised to her at marriage) worth Rs. 200,000 plus gold ornaments and a house share. The trial court dissolved the marriage but didn't clearly state whether it was granting a "khula" (wife-initiated divorce, which under Islamic law can require the wife to give up her dower). The husband later argued in the High Court that since it was effectively a khula, his wife should forfeit her right to the dower money—and the High Court agreed, denying her the Rs. 200,000.

The Supreme Court, in this order, granted leave to appeal, meaning it agreed to seriously review the case rather than reject it. The Court raised several important legal questions: whether the trial court's findings actually supported a khula ruling, whether dower is automatically forfeited in a khula divorce, whether the wife could still defend her case even if she hadn't formally appealed one specific finding, and whether the High Court could decide on the dower issue at all while a related appeal was already pending elsewhere.

This case matters because it addresses how courts should determine whether a divorce counts as khula, and whether women automatically lose financial rights (like dower) in such cases—an issue affecting family law rights across Pakistan.

title: Time period for restoring suit dismissed in default
explainer:
This case involved a custody dispute where a father (Sikandar Ali) was seeking to overturn an ex-parte (one-sided) custody decree granted to the mother (Robina Kousar) for their minor child.

Background: A custody decree was issued against the father on 18.3.2004 without his participation. He later filed a petition to set this aside, but that petition was dismissed for non-prosecution (failure to pursue the case) on 5.1.2005. An earlier attempt to restore that petition had already failed. He then filed another restoration application on 10.6.2005 — over five months after the dismissal — claiming his junior lawyer had misunderstood which cases were scheduled for hearing.

The Court's Decision: The AJ&K High Court upheld the lower court's dismissal. Under Rule XII(II) of the Family Court Procedural Rules, 1998, a court can restore a case dismissed for default only if the restoration application is filed within 30 days and shows sufficient cause. Here, the father's application came five months late, with no explanation for the delay and no application to excuse it. His claim about his lawyer's confusion was unsupported by any affidavit. The Court also noted his own petition admitted an earlier restoration attempt had already failed and become final.

Why it matters: This case confirms that strict time limits apply to restoring dismissed cases in family court, and that vague excuses without evidence (like affidavits) or formal delay-condonation requests won't succeed—even in sensitive matters like child custody.

**What was this case about?**

A husband (Dr. Ejaz Naseem) filed a case for restitution of conjugal rights against his wife (Fareeha Ahmad). In response, the wife filed a written statement seeking divorce through khula, plus recovery of money, jewelry, household goods, maintenance for herself and her two daughters, and educational/maternity expenses. Before evidence was recorded, both parties reached a compromise, and the Family Court passed a decree in 2005 based on that agreement—granting divorce and the wife's other claims.

Later, when the wife tried to enforce (execute) this decree, the husband objected, then appealed—390 days late. He argued that the Family Court never had the legal power (jurisdiction) to decide claims like money, jewelry, and expenses based on a written statement; only khula could be claimed that way, and consent between parties cannot create jurisdiction that the law doesn't provide.

**What did the Supreme Court decide?**

The Court rejected his argument. It held that Section 5 of the Family Courts Act gives Family Courts exclusive jurisdiction over all matters listed in the Act's Schedule—including divorce, dower, maintenance, custody, dowry, and personal property—regardless of whether they're raised as claims or counter-claims. Since the husband never objected to jurisdiction earlier and had voluntarily agreed to the compromise, he was estopped (legally barred) from challenging it now. His 390-day-late appeal was also rightly rejected.

title: Ingredients of a Benami Transactions
explainer:
**Case Summary: Benami Transaction Dispute**

This case involved a property dispute between Qurib Ali and his brother's family (respondents) over land that was officially registered in the name of Qurib Ali's brother, Muhammad Chuttal.

**Background:** Qurib Ali worked for the former Khairpur State government. During his employment, government rules barred civil servants from purchasing land in their own names without permission. To get around this restriction, he bought land but registered it in his brother's name—this is called a "benami" transaction, where the person who actually pays for and owns property registers it under someone else's name.

Qurib Ali claimed he paid the full purchase price, kept possession of the land, held the original title documents, and paid all government taxes on the property. After being forcibly removed from the land, he sued to be recognized as the true owner. Both the trial court and the High Court initially rejected his claim, saying he lacked sufficient documentary proof.

**Supreme Court's Intervention:** The Supreme Court sent the case back, clarifying that documentary evidence isn't always necessary to prove a benami transaction—courts should look at the whole picture.

**Final Decision:** On review, the High Court ruled in Qurib Ali's favor. It found that the source of payment, possession of documents, physical possession of the land, and his motive (avoiding the government service ban) all proved he was the real owner. The Court restored his ownership and ordered compensation for lost profits.

**Why it matters:** This case clarifies the legal test for identifying benami transactions

title: When a child is legal?
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

A man (the petitioner) was ordered by a Family Court to pay maintenance (financial support) to two children. He challenged this order in the Lahore High Court, denying that he was the father of the minors. He claimed the children were actually born from the mother's previous husband, not from him.

**What did the court find?**

The High Court examined the evidence and found that the man and woman had lived together as husband and wife, and the children were born during this cohabitation. The woman had consistently maintained that she was his legally wedded wife. Importantly, the man never filed a legal case (called a "suit for jactitation of marriage") to formally dispute or disprove her claim of marriage — something he could have done if he genuinely believed the marriage wasn't valid. The court also noted that he had previously sent maintenance money for the children through money order while they lived in another city, which contradicted his denial of paternity.

**What did the court decide?**

The High Court ruled that the children were legitimate offspring of the man, born from a lawful marital union. It dismissed his petition, upheld the maintenance order, and even imposed additional costs on him — criticizing his conduct as "shameful" for trying to avoid his legal and moral duty to support his own children.

**Why it matters:**

This case shows how courts determine a child's legitimacy using evidence of cohabitation and marital status, and reinforces that fathers cannot evade financial responsibility for their children through denial alone.

title: NEPRA REGULATIONS, 2012
explainer:
This is not a court judgment—it is a set of procedural regulations (subordinate legislation) issued by Pakistan's National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (NEPRA) in 2012, under powers granted by the Regulation of Generation, Transmission and Distribution of Electric Power Act, 1997.

The regulations establish the process for filing appeals before NEPRA against decisions of a single Member of the Authority, the Tribunal, or a Provincial Inspection office. Key rules include: appeals must be filed within 30 days of the order (with provision for delay if there's sufficient cause); appeals must be sent by registered post or courier to the Registrar, accompanied by a verified affidavit, a certified copy of the challenged order, and a Rs. 1,000 fee; documents must be typed, paginated, and submitted in four sets. The regulations also detail how the Registrar screens appeals for defects, how notice is given to the opposing party (respondent), how respondents may reply within 10 days, and how hearings and adjournments are handled—including dismissal of an appeal if the appellant doesn't show up, subject to restoration on valid grounds.

This matters because it creates a clear, standardized procedure for consumers, licensees, or other affected parties to challenge electricity-related regulatory decisions, ensuring fairness, transparency, and timely resolution of disputes within Pakistan's electric power regulatory system. # Can a Government Employee Break a Scholarship Bond to Take a University Job?

**What the case was about:**

This case involved a man convicted by a trial court for an offence related to zina (unlawful sexual relations) under Pakistan's Hudood Ordinance. The trial court convicted him under Section 10(2) of the Zina Ordinance and sentenced him to seven years in prison plus a fine.

The court also noted suspicious conduct by witnesses and missing evidentiary links.

Because the abduction element wasn't proven and evidence of marriage created reasonable doubt, the court gave the accused the benefit of the doubt and accepted his appeal, meaning his conviction was overturned.

title: No person can have favorite portion in joint property without consent of others
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

A group of relatives (respondents) who were recorded as co-owners in revenue records filed a suit demanding possession of their share in jointly-owned property through partition. The petitioners, who were in possession of the land, contested this. Both the trial court and the first appellate court ruled in favor of the respondents, confirming their ownership shares and ordering partition. The petitioners then challenged these decisions before the Peshawar High Court, arguing that not all co-owners were made parties to the suit and that the courts had ignored evidence and legal objections they had raised.

**What did the court decide?**

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that the revenue records clearly showed the respondents as co-owners, and the petitioners never disputed this in their pleadings or claimed sole ownership of the property. Since parties cannot argue points at trial that weren't raised in their pleadings, this objection failed. The court also clarified that while a preliminary decree for partition was rightly passed, all co-owners must eventually be joined before a final decree distributing specific plots is issued.

**Why does it matter?**

The judgment reinforces a key principle of property law: no co-owner can unilaterally occupy or claim a specific, favorable portion of jointly-owned land just because of informal family arrangements or long-standing possession. Without the consent of all co-owners and proper legal partition proceedings, such arrangements don't create ownership rights. This protects the equal rights of all co-owners in shared property.

This case arose from a false criminal accusation. A man named Muhammad Saeed and a woman, Mst. Zarin Khatoon, had married each other by their own consent. However, some relatives of the woman filed a police case claiming Saeed and others had forcibly abducted her, invoking the harsh Zina (Enforcement of Hadood) Ordinance, 1979 — a charge carrying life imprisonment.

The trial court acquitted the accused, giving them the benefit of the doubt. When the case reached the Federal Shariat Court on appeal, the Court found overwhelming evidence that Zarin Khatoon and Saeed had genuinely married and lived as husband and wife months before the alleged "abduction" date. The witnesses who claimed abduction had given self-contradictory and knowingly false statements to fabricate a case against multiple innocent people, including even the cleric who performed the marriage.

The Court held that producing a formal marriage certificate (Nikahnama) isn't essential to prove marriage — the couple's own consistent claim of being husband and wife is enough. More importantly, it ruled that deliberately fabricating false abduction allegations amounts to perjury and fabricating evidence under the Pakistan Penal Code (Sections 193 and 195), especially serious because it sought to send innocent people to prison for life on a false charge.

As a result, three of the false witnesses were convicted of perjury and sentenced to three years' rigorous imprisonment each.

title: Powers to Conduct Audit
explainer:
Laraib Energy Limited, a company operating a hydroelectric power complex, challenged notices issued by tax officers (Commissioner and Additional Commissioner Inland Revenue) asking it to produce records for an audit of its sales tax and federal excise affairs. The company argued that only the Board of Revenue—not the Commissioner—had the power under Section 72B of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, to select taxpayers for audit. It relied on a Lahore High Court ruling supporting this view.

The tax authorities countered that Section 25 of the same Act separately empowered the Commissioner and Inland Revenue officers to access records and conduct audits, independent of the Board's selection power under Section 72B. They pointed to a clarifying "Explanation" added to the law and a similar case from the Islamabad High Court that upheld such notices.

The Azad Jammu & Kashmir High Court agreed with the tax authorities. It held that the Commissioner's power under Section 25 (and similarly under the Income Tax Ordinance) to call for records and conduct audits is separate from the Board's power under Section 72B. The Court reasoned that self-assessment by taxpayers isn't beyond verification, and tax laws shouldn't be interpreted to add restrictions not clearly stated. Finding no merit in the company's arguments, the Court dismissed the petition outright.

This case matters because it clarifies that tax officers can independently exercise audit powers without needing prior selection by the central Board of Revenue.

title: Quashment in a Drugs Act 1976 case
explainer:
**What the case was about:**

This case involved two employees of a pharmaceutical company (a Quality Control Incharge and a Warrantor) who were being prosecuted under Pakistan's Drugs Act, 1976, after a drug sample (Renuvit capsules) was found to be "substandard and misbranded" by a government laboratory. The accused had asked the trial court (Drug Court, Balochistan) to dismiss the case against them before trial, but their request was rejected. They then approached the High Court seeking to have the entire case quashed.

**What the court decided:**

The Balochistan High Court accepted the petition and quashed the proceedings, for two main reasons:

1. **The company itself was never prosecuted** — only its employees were. Citing Supreme Court precedent, the court held that employees cannot be held liable unless the company is first found guilty; since the company wasn't even a party to the case, this was fatal to the prosecution.

2. **The lab report was dangerously late.** The law requires analysis reports within 60 days, with any delay formally justified in writing. Here, the report took over nine months, with no explanation given. The court called this a violation of a "mandatory" legal requirement, meaning no conviction could be based on it.

**Why it matters:**

The ruling reinforces that procedural safeguards under the Drugs Act—like timely testing and proper accountability of companies before their employees—must be strictly followed. Courts can quash cases early if there's no realistic chance of conviction, sparing accused persons from pointless trials.

explainer:
This case is about a long-running dispute over a petrol pump/CNG station site in Islamabad, leased by the Capital Development Authority (CDA) through its Staff Welfare Organization to Mr. S.M. Ismail in 1973 for 30 years.

When the lease neared its end, CDA offered only a 5-year extension at a much higher rent. Ismail didn't reject this outright but instead asked for a full 30-year renewal, similar to what CDA itself enjoyed. Instead of responding properly, CDA later forcibly dispossessed him and sealed his premises without following proper legal procedure or giving prior notice.

The Lahore High Court (Rawalpindi Bench) ruled that:

1. Ismail's petition to the High Court was valid, since he was dispossessed without required legal notice.
2. Government bodies must act fairly and lawfully, and courts can step in when they don't.
3. Since this was a lease (not a rent-controlled tenancy), the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction — this was a landlord-tenant lease matter, not one covered by rent laws.
4. CDA's dispossession of Ismail was illegal and done in bad faith ("arrogant" and "malicious"), especially since CDA itself benefited from long renewable leases but denied the same fairness to Ismail.

The Court ordered Ismail's possession restored and directed CDA to extend his lease for another 30 years, applying principles of equity and fairness.

title: Technicalities would be avoided and matter would be decided on Merit
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over maintenance (financial support) payments in Multan. The wife had sued her husband for maintenance for herself and their four children (two daughters and two sons). When the husband stopped participating in the case, the court passed an ex-parte (one-sided) decree against him, ordering him to pay maintenance for all four children and his wife.

The husband filed an application to set aside this ex-parte decree, and evidence was actually recorded in his favor. However, he later missed a hearing, and his application was dismissed for "non-prosecution" (failure to pursue the case) rather than being decided on its actual merits. When he asked the court to restore his application, that request was also rejected. An appeal to a higher court also failed.

The Lahore High Court found this troubling, especially since the two adult sons appeared in court supporting their father, claiming they had been living with him all along—meaning their mother may have wrongly claimed maintenance for them.

The High Court ruled that cases should be decided on their merits (the actual facts and evidence) rather than dismissed on technical grounds like missed appearances. It set aside the lower courts' rulings and ordered the case to be reconsidered properly, with evidence examined, within two months—though the husband first had to pay any overdue maintenance for the daughters.

This case matters because it reinforces that courts should prioritize fair, evidence-based decisions over rigid procedural technicalities.

Two men (Muhammad Ramzan and another) were named in a police case (FIR) accusing them of dacoity (armed robbery) under Section 392 of the Pakistan Penal Code. title: Procedure when defendant is in Jail
explainer:
Here's a plain-language explainer:

**What the case was about:**
Muhammad Nazir sued Shafqat Mehmood to recover Rs. 38,80,000 based on a cheque, using a special fast-track court procedure (Order XXXVII CPC) for cheque-recovery cases. At the time the suit was filed, Mehmood was in jail on an unrelated criminal case. The court tried to serve him legal notice through the jail superintendent, but this failed, so the court eventually resorted to publishing a public notice in a newspaper. A lawyer then filed papers on Mehmood's behalf seeking permission to defend the suit — but the trial court rejected this application, ruling it was filed too late (after the 10-day legal deadline).

**What the court decided:**
The Lahore High Court disagreed. It found that Mehmood was never properly served according to law while he was in jail — publishing a newspaper notice for someone in custody was impractical and improper. Since proper service never happened, the 10-day clock for responding hadn't actually started running. The court ruled that when someone is in jail, the law requires proper steps (like producing him from jail for service) — skipping these isn't a mere technicality but a real legal failure. The petition was accepted, meaning Mehmood's request to defend himself would go forward.

**Why it matters:**
This case reinforces that courts must follow proper service procedures, especially for jailed defendants, and should prioritize real justice over rigid technical dismissals when someone was unable to respond through no fault of their own.

title: Theft case Bail Granted after Partial Recovery
explainer:
**What was this case about?**

Six men (Muhammad Madni and others) were accused of stealing two buffaloes, two calves, and two cows belonging to a complainant. A First Information Report (FIR) was registered against them under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with theft (Section 380), giving false information to mislead an investigation (Section 215), and dishonestly receiving stolen property (Section 411). The police claimed to have recovered one buffalo and one calf from the accused. The men had been in jail since July 2013 and sought "post-arrest bail" — meaning release while their trial proceeds.

**What did the court decide?**

The Lahore High Court (Multan Bench) granted them bail. The judge noted that although police claimed a recovery of animals, the recovery memo showed it was a "joint recovery" — meaning the property was recovered from multiple accused together rather than pinpointed to a specific individual through their own disclosure. Courts generally consider such joint recoveries weak evidence, as they don't clearly establish which specific accused led police to the stolen goods. The court also noted the alleged offense wasn't among the serious crimes barred from bail under Section 497 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

**Why does it matter?**

This case illustrates an important legal principle: recovery evidence attributed jointly to several accused, rather than individually, carries little weight in Pakistani courts. It also shows how bail is often granted for offenses not classified as most serious, especially when evidence against the accused appears weak.

# Case Explainer: Amjad Ali and Others v. Anwar Shah and Others (PLJ 2015)

**What was this case about?**

This dispute centered on a house in Peshawar. The original plaintiff, Khalil Khan, claimed he owned the house and that Haji Yar Badshah was his tenant who paid rent (called "Khak Shora"). Khalil Khan filed a lawsuit to evict Yar Badshah and take possession of the property.

However, the situation became complicated. Yar Badshah had earlier filed his own lawsuit claiming he owned the property through "adverse possession" (a legal claim based on long-term occupation), but that suit was dismissed. After Yar Badshah died, his sons (the respondents) were brought into the case as his legal heirs. But they also claimed a *separate* right to the property—they said they had independently purchased shares in it through official land mutations and a registered sale deed, making them co-owners, not just tenants' heirs.

**What did the Court decide?**

The Peshawar High Court dismissed the petition, upholding the lower appellate court's decision to reject the eviction claim. The plaintiff failed to prove: (1) that a landlord-tenant relationship actually existed, (2) which specific portion of the property was being rented, and (3) that rent payments were ever made. The Court also noted the respondents had legitimately purchased ownership shares *before* the eviction suit was even filed.

**Why does this matter?**

The judgment clarifies that tenancy rights don't
